13-coins.descriptor: All-day American-Italian restaurant in Pioneer Square

14-carrot-cafe.text: A family-run Eastlake breakfast institution open since 1977, in the Hines Public Market Building — the menu runs to carrot cake pancakes, carrot juice and "Tahitian" French toast made with tahini. USA Today named it one of Seattle's ten best cafes in 2017.
14-carrot-cafe.descriptor: Eastlake breakfast cafe since 1977, known for carrot cake pancakes

5-spot.text: The 5 Spot is a Queen Anne breakfast institution, serving breakfast all day alongside diner comfort food like mac and cheese, burgers and nachos. Seattle Times readers voted it Best Breakfast in Seattle three years running — 2023, 2024 and 2025.
5-spot.descriptor: All-day American breakfast spot on Queen Anne Ave N

5th-avenue-theater.text: Opened September 24, 1926, the 5th Avenue's interior is a Chinese-inspired fantasy by architect Robert C. Reamer, whose team worked from a 1925 illustrated survey of Chinese architecture — an octagonal coffered ceiling with a sculpted five-toed imperial dragon above the chandelier, modeled on the throne room of the Forbidden City's Hall of Supreme Harmony. It's also a Broadway proving ground: Hairspray, Shrek the Musical, Memphis and Aladdin all had early runs here.
5th-avenue-theater.descriptor: 1926 Broadway house at 1308 5th Ave with a Chinese-inspired interior

a-hong-kong-kitchen.text: A Hong Kong–style kitchen in the Chinatown–International District, serving the Cantonese canon — dim sum, roast meats, and noodle plates like beef brisket and shrimp lo mein — a few blocks off South Jackson.
a-hong-kong-kitchen.descriptor: Hong Kong–style Cantonese restaurant in the Chinatown-ID

act-theatre.text: Gregory Falls founded ACT in 1965, and since 1996 it has occupied Kreielsheimer Place inside the Eagles Auditorium Building, built in 1924-25 — a National Register landmark where Martin Luther King Jr. spoke in 1961 and the Grateful Dead played eight times in 1967-68. In 2025 ACT merged with Seattle Shakespeare Company to form the Union Arts Center.
act-theatre.descriptor: Nonprofit theater in the 1920s Eagles Auditorium Building on Union St

agua-verde-cafe.text: The taqueria sits above the Agua Verde Paddle Club, which has rented kayaks off this Portage Bay dock since 1997. The order is Baja-style tacos on house-made tortillas with a view of boats going by, and then a paddle out toward the Montlake Cut and the Arboretum.
agua-verde-cafe.descriptor: Baja-style taqueria above a kayak dock on Portage Bay

aladdin-gyro-cery-deli.text: A cheap, fast U District standby on the Ave, singled out among the neighborhood's several falafel counters for crisp falafel and its tahini sauce, with a back area of couches and tables if you want to linger.
aladdin-gyro-cery-deli.descriptor: Greek-Mediterranean gyro and falafel counter at 4139 University Way NE

alibi-room.text: A speakeasy-feeling hideaway tucked into Post Alley directly across from the Gum Wall, the Alibi Room has long been a hangout for Northwest writers, authors and artists. The brick-and-beam room is known for brick-oven pizzas and cocktails, with the kitchen running until 1 a.m.
alibi-room.descriptor: Post Alley hideaway bar across from the Gum Wall, brick-oven pizza

alki-beach-park.text: The Denny Party came ashore at Alki Point on November 13, 1851 and named the settlement New York Alki — "alki" being Chinook Jargon for "by and by." Arthur Denny soon moved to the east shore of Elliott Bay, the site that became Pioneer Square. The beach still carries the Birthplace of Seattle monument and a scale replica of the Statue of Liberty donated in 1952.
alki-beach-park.descriptor: West Seattle beach where the city's founders landed in 1851

allegro-coffee.descriptor: Coffee and juice bar inside the Interbay Whole Foods on 15th Ave W

altura.text: Nathan Lockwood cooked at San Francisco's Acquerello and Fleur de Lys before he and his wife opened Altura on Broadway E in 2011. It's tasting-menu only — Italian technique applied to Pacific Northwest ingredients from local foragers, fishermen and farmers — served from an open kitchen. The couple also runs Carrello across the street.
altura.descriptor: Italian-leaning tasting-menu fine dining on Broadway E, Capitol Hill

analog-coffee.descriptor: Capitol Hill coffee shop on Summit Ave E

anchorhead-coffee.text: Anchorhead was started by Jake Paulson and Mike Steiner and won America's Best Espresso at Coffee Fest Portland in 2015. Its signature pastry is the "quaffle" — part cinnamon roll, part croissant, part waffle — and the downtown bar is one of several Seattle shops supplied by the company's roastery in Duvall.
anchorhead-coffee.descriptor: Local espresso roaster's downtown cafe, known for the 'quaffle' pastry

anchorhead-coffee-co.text: Anchorhead was founded by Jake Paulson and Mike Steiner and won America's Best Espresso at Coffee Fest Portland in 2015. It's also home of the "quaffle" — part cinnamon roll, part croissant, part waffle.
anchorhead-coffee-co.descriptor: Specialty roaster's cafe on Western Ave near Pike Place Market

anchorhead-coffee-downtown-7th-avenue.text: Anchorhead was founded by Jake Paulson and Mike Steiner, roasting in Duvall and pouring at cafes around the Seattle area and beyond. It won America's Best Espresso at Coffee Fest Portland in 2015, and is nearly as well known for the quaffle — part cinnamon roll, part croissant, part waffle. This is the 12th Ave cafe, not one of the two downtown bars.
anchorhead-coffee-downtown-7th-avenue.descriptor: Specialty roaster's cafe on 12th Ave, home of the "quaffle"

annapurna-cafe.text: Chef-owner Roshita Shrestha's underground Broadway dining room serves Himalayan food spanning Nepal, India and Tibet, with spinach momo dumplings and their peanut, sesame and tomato dipping sauces as the calling card. Seattle Weekly named it Best Indian Food in Seattle in 2012, and it added the Yeti Bar in 2015.
annapurna-cafe.descriptor: Basement Nepali-Tibetan-Indian spot on Broadway, known for momos

anthonys-pier-66.text: Budd Gould's Anthony's began as a Bellevue prime rib house in 1973 and added its own wholesale seafood company at Pier 91 in 1984, buying straight from fishermen in the Northwest, Alaska and Hawaii. The Pier 66 building on the downtown waterfront stacks three restaurants in one: the flagship dining room on the second floor, the casual Bell Street Diner below it, and a walk-up Fish Bar at street level.
anthonys-pier-66.descriptor: Northwest seafood at Pier 66 on the downtown Seattle waterfront

arashi-ramen-ballard.descriptor: Tonkotsu ramen shop at 5401 20th Ave NW in Ballard

arayas-place.text: One of Seattle's longest-running vegan kitchens, open since 1987 and named for the founders' mother, Araya, whose travels abroad shaped the family's cooking. Everything is plant-based and Thai, served under the house line "vegetables taste better here."
arayas-place.descriptor: All-vegan Thai restaurant and bar on University Way NE since 1987

arepa-venezuelan-kitchen.text: Isamary Herrera was born in Mérida, Venezuela and learned to make arepas from her mother at age 10 before immigrating to Seattle in 2001; in 2022 she and her husband Ulises Andrade bought this U District restaurant from its founder, Felix Valderrama. The bestseller is the pabellón arepa: shredded beef, black beans, fried plantains and cheese.
arepa-venezuelan-kitchen.descriptor: Venezuelan arepas and empanadas in the University District

argosy-cruises.text: The family-owned company started more than 76 years ago as the Spring Street Water Taxi and spent years as Seattle Harbor Tours before becoming Argosy. Its one-hour harbor cruise loops Elliott Bay from Pier 55 on the downtown waterfront, and Argosy also runs the annual Christmas Ship Festival.
argosy-cruises.descriptor: Elliott Bay harbor cruises from Pier 55 on the downtown waterfront

argosy-cruises-lake-union.text: Argosy has run Seattle sightseeing boats since 1949. The two-hour Locks Cruise leaves this South Lake Union dock and passes floating homes, seaplanes and Gas Works Park before dropping to Puget Sound through the Ballard Locks — the "boat elevator" — after ducking under the city's drawbridges.
argosy-cruises-lake-union.descriptor: Two-hour Ballard Locks sightseeing cruise from the AGC Marina dock

artusi.text: Artusi is the cocktail-and-amaro bar attached to Spinasse, the Piedmontese restaurant next door that opened on Capitol Hill in 2008. It takes its name from Pellegrino Artusi, whose 1891 cookbook collected recipes from across Italy and is credited with helping forge a single national cuisine.
artusi.descriptor: Italian aperitivo and amaro bar on 14th Ave, next door to Spinasse

asadero-ballard.text: Asadero Sinaloa opened its Ballard outpost in September 2016 in the old Zayda Buddy's space, bringing over the wood-fired Sonoran beef, house-made flour tortillas and stone-ground salsas that had made its original Kent restaurant a destination. The bigger Leary Ave room added Sinaloan seafood, including fish tacos grilled over mesquite.
asadero-ballard.descriptor: Northern Mexican mesquite-grill steakhouse on Leary Ave in Ballard

assaggio-ristorante.text: Chef Mauro Golmarvi learned to cook as a boy in Rome and later moved to Ancona for medical school before chasing a cooking career to America. When he opened Assaggio in 1993 he finally got the dining room he'd always pictured: hand-painted frescoes inspired by the Sistine Chapel.
assaggio-ristorante.descriptor: Italian restaurant on 4th Ave in Belltown, open since 1993

aurora-avenue-north.text: Aurora Avenue is Seattle's leg of State Route 99, the old Pacific Highway and the main north-south route before I-5. It carries the 1932 George Washington Memorial Bridge — the Aurora Bridge — 167 feet above the Ship Canal, and the expressway was cut through Woodland Park in 1933 over public objections.
aurora-avenue-north.descriptor: Seattle's stretch of State Route 99, the old Pacific Highway

ba-bar.text: Ba Bar is chef Eric Banh's more casual counterpart to Monsoon, serving Vietnamese street food on 12th Ave — phở, vermicelli bowls, rotisserie chicken, duck and pork belly, pandan cake and Vietnamese coffee. It has been listed among the city's essential late-night restaurants, and the South Lake Union sibling later spun off a vegan walk-up window, Ba Bar Green, in 2022.
ba-bar.descriptor: Vietnamese street food and phở on 12th Ave from chef Eric Banh

ba-bar-minor.text: Ba Bar comes from siblings Eric and Sophie Banh, whose Saigon Siblings group also runs Monsoon, the Capitol Hill Vietnamese restaurant they opened in 1999. The menu runs to pho, vermicelli bowls, rotisserie chicken, duck and pork belly, pandan cake and Vietnamese coffee; in 2022 the South Lake Union location added Ba Bar Green, a walk-up window serving vegan food.
ba-bar-minor.descriptor: Vietnamese street food and pho in South Lake Union

bagel-oasis.descriptor: Bagel shop and café on NE 65th St in Ravenna

bahn-thai.text: Bahn Thai has been in the orange house-like building on Roy Street in lower Queen Anne since 1984, which makes it the oldest Thai restaurant in Seattle. It was started by the uncles of current co-owner Sean Ekavithvorakul, who took over running it after his father died in 2020 — the place still keeps no social media and runs largely on four decades of regulars.
bahn-thai.descriptor: Thai restaurant on Roy Street in lower Queen Anne, open since 1984

ballard-commons-park.text: Ballard's public park and town square, beside the neighbourhood's library and Civic Center. It closed at the end of 2021 and reopened in March 2023 after a redesign.
ballard-commons-park.descriptor: Public park and town square in Seattle's Ballard neighborhood

bangrak-market.text: A Belltown kitchen and bar serving Thai street-market food — the menu is built on the idea that market food is comfort food and the soul of a community — and it stays open until 2am on Friday and Saturday nights.
bangrak-market.descriptor: Belltown Thai street-food restaurant and bar on 2nd Ave

bar-del-corso.text: Chef Jerry Corso and Angelina Tolentino opened Bar del Corso on Beacon Avenue in July 2011, and it became the neighborhood restaurant other neighborhoods envy — a short menu of wood-fired pizza and Italian small plates that has landed it on best-of-Seattle lists from Condé Nast Traveler, Time Out and Seattle Met.
bar-del-corso.descriptor: Wood-fired pizza and Italian small plates on Beacon Hill since 2011

barnacle.text: Barnacle is essentially one long wooden bar at 4743 Ballard Ave NW, sharing the address with Renee Erickson's oyster restaurant The Walrus and the Carpenter, which opened there in 2010. The local move is to drink and eat a few oysters here while you wait for a table next door.
barnacle.descriptor: Tiny bar on Ballard Ave, sister to The Walrus and the Carpenter

barolo-ristorante.text: Barolo is run by brothers Leo, Salvio and Roberto Varchetta, the family behind Mamma Melina in the U District and Cinque Terre on Westlake, who have been cooking Italian in Seattle for over 30 years. The room is the draw as much as the pasta: a 19-foot walnut communal table, 16-foot wine display cases and ornate glass chandeliers, a design that took a 2007 AIA/IIDA hospitality honors award.
barolo-ristorante.descriptor: Upscale Italian on Westlake Ave from the Varchetta family

bathtub-gin.text: Bathtub Gin & Co. is tucked into the former boiler room of the Humphrey Building, a terra-cotta apartment house designed by Warren Milner and completed in 1928 — one of the largest pre-1930 buildings left in Belltown. The entrance is deliberately unmarked so the bar feels discovered rather than announced, and the Prohibition-era name matches a classics-driven cocktail list.
bathtub-gin.descriptor: Hidden Prohibition-style cocktail bar in a Belltown boiler room

benaroya-hall.text: Benaroya Hall opened in September 1998 as the Seattle Symphony's home, sitting atop the Great Northern rail tunnel and beside the downtown transit tunnel — so the 2,500-seat main auditorium floats on rubber pads that isolate it from the rest of the building. The lobby holds Dale Chihuly glass, including Crystal Cascade.
benaroya-hall.descriptor: Seattle Symphony's downtown concert hall at 200 University St, opened 1998

beneath-the-streets.text: After the Great Fire of 1889, Seattle rebuilt Pioneer Square and raised the street grade, turning old ground-floor storefronts into buried basements and leaving hollow passageways under the sidewalks. The city closed them in 1907 over bubonic plague fears; Beneath the Streets has run tours of the surviving stretches since 2013.
beneath-the-streets.descriptor: Underground history tour starting on Cherry St in Pioneer Square

beths-cafe.text: Beth's opened on Aurora Avenue by Green Lake in 1954 — it started out as a nickel-slot gambling parlor and added food to keep customers around. The 12-egg omelet arrives on a pizza tray with bottomless hash browns; the host of Man v. Food couldn't finish one in 2009. Customers' crayon drawings cover the walls and get taken down and archived every January.
beths-cafe.descriptor: 24-hour Aurora Ave diner famous for its 12-egg omelet

biang-biang-noodles.text: The shop's namesake is a Shaanxi specialty out of Xi'an: thick, belt-wide noodles pulled by hand and slapped against the table — the slap is what the onomatopoeic word 'biang' imitates. The character used to write it runs 58 strokes in its traditional form, one of the most complex in modern Chinese, and it only got a Unicode slot in 2020.
biang-biang-noodles.descriptor: Hand-pulled Shaanxi biang biang noodles at 601 E Pike, Capitol Hill

big-marios-pizza.text: Big Mario's opened on Capitol Hill in 2010 and grew to three Seattle locations. It's the divey late-night slice shop for big New York-style cheese slices with curled pepperoni cups, plus oddball whole pies like macaroni and cheese or pear and gorgonzola.
big-marios-pizza.descriptor: New York-style pizza by the slice on E Pike, Capitol Hill since 2010

big-marios-pizza-fremont.text: Big Mario's began on Capitol Hill in 2010 selling New York-style slices and whole pies alongside off-script versions like macaroni and cheese, potato and pesto, and pear gorgonzola. It added a Lower Queen Anne shop in 2015 plus this one on Leary Way NW, and is known as a divey spot with a small backroom bar.
big-marios-pizza-fremont.descriptor: New York-style pizza by the slice on Leary Way NW

big-marios-pizza-uptown.text: Big Mario's started on Capitol Hill in 2010 with big, cheesy New York-style slices — the ones with curled pepperoni cups — and a late-night reputation; the Queen Anne shop followed in 2015. The whole-pie list runs to oddities like macaroni and cheese, potato pesto, and the Mai Tai with Italian ham and pineapple.
big-marios-pizza-uptown.descriptor: New York-style pizza by the slice in Uptown/Lower Queen Anne since 2015

big-time-brewery-and-alehouse.text: Big Time was founded in December 1988 on The Ave in the University District and has long been billed as Seattle's original brewpub — guidebooks used that exact tag by the mid-2000s. It is still family-owned, crafts its own beers, and has been a neighborhood staple for more than three decades.
big-time-brewery-and-alehouse.descriptor: Brewpub on The Ave in the U District, brewing since 1988

bimbos-cantina.descriptor: Mexican street-taco spot on E Pike, above the Cha Cha Lounge

birthplace-of-seattle.text: On November 13, 1851 the Denny Party came ashore here and named their settlement "New York Alki" — Chinook Jargon for "by and by." By April 1852 Arthur Denny had moved across Elliott Bay to the site of Pioneer Square, and most of the colonists followed. The monument, dedicated on the landing's anniversary in 1905, lists the founders: Arthur Denny, John Low, Carson Boren, David Denny and Charles Terry.
birthplace-of-seattle.descriptor: Alki Beach monument marking the Denny Party's 1851 landing

biscuit-bitch.text: Kimmie Spice's "trailer park to table" cafe piles gravy-drenched biscuits with garlic grits, hot links and pork sausage, and Seattle Metropolitan named it among the city's best biscuits in 2022. Lizzo stopped in at the First Avenue shop in 2019 for a post-concert breakfast.
biscuit-bitch.descriptor: Cajun-Creole biscuits-and-gravy cafe near Pike Place Market

biscuit-bitch-belltown.text: Kimmie Spice's self-described "trailer park to table" cafe built its name on gravy-drenched biscuits loaded with garlic grits, hot links and pork sausage — what Seattle Met files under hangover cures. The chain contracted to Belltown and Pike Place after its Pioneer Square and White Center shops closed in 2020, and Lizzo stopped in at the First Avenue location after Capitol Hill Block Party in 2019.

bizzarro.text: Bizzarro has occupied a converted 1920s auto garage in Wallingford since 1986, when visual artist David Nast and his artist friends fitted it out on almost no budget. Carnival props, a bicycle and a small forest of chandeliers hang from the ceiling — one reviewer called it part circus horror-movie set, part red-sauce Italian joint — and it was long known for a server who improvised opera about your pasta.
bizzarro.descriptor: Wallingford Italian cafe with handmade pasta and carnival-junk decor, since 1986

black-bottle.text: An independently owned Belltown gastrotavern on the corner of 1st and Vine, open since 2005 and built around a wide variety of shareable plates rather than entrees. It's 21-and-over, and the house tagline is "more flavor than flash."
black-bottle.descriptor: Belltown gastrotavern at 1st and Vine, shared plates since 2005

bongos-caribbean-cafe.text: Bongos took over a former gas station on Aurora and leaned all the way in: where the pumps once stood there's now a sand-pit patio, so you can eat jerk chicken with your feet in the sand even in a gray Seattle winter.
bongos-caribbean-cafe.descriptor: Caribbean café in a converted gas station on Aurora Ave N

boon-boona-coffee.text: Boon Boona sources and roasts coffee exclusively from African producers — founder Efrem Fesaha started it in 2019, inspired by his family's ties to Eritrea — and directs a larger share of profits to mainly women-owned growers. At the original Renton store you can still sit for an Ethiopian coffee ceremony, green beans pan-roasted and brewed in a clay pot called a jebena.
boon-boona-coffee.descriptor: East African coffee cafe and roaster on E Cherry St

brimmer-heeltap.text: The name is two old British drinking words: a "brimmer" is a glass filled to the rim, a "heeltap" the last drops left at the bottom. Jen Doak opened it in late 2013 in the Ballard space that had long been the French restaurant Le Gourmand, and the garden patio out back is the reason regulars keep coming.
brimmer-heeltap.descriptor: Seasonal small plates and a garden patio at 425 NW Market St, Ballard

bruce-and-brandon-lee-graves.text: Martial artist Bruce Lee was buried at Lake View Cemetery in 1973; his son Brandon, who died in 1993, lies beside him. The graves draw thousands of visitors a year and were listed by Time among the top 10 celebrity graves in the world. The 1872 cemetery also holds Denny Party pioneers, Nordstrom founder John W. Nordstrom, and Princess Angeline, daughter of Chief Seattle.
bruce-and-brandon-lee-graves.descriptor: Bruce and Brandon Lee's side-by-side graves in Lake View Cemetery, Capitol Hill

buddha-ruksa.text: Michael and Nui moved to West Seattle in 2000 and opened Buddha Ruksa on Genesee Street on January 6, 2003. The restaurant is named for a flower, and like it the kitchen keeps blossoming — adapting Thai cooking to the present rather than guarding secret recipes.
buddha-ruksa.descriptor: Thai restaurant on SW Genesee St in West Seattle since 2003

burke-museum-of-natural-history-and-cult.text: Founded in 1899 and run by the University of Washington, the Burke holds more than 16 million objects, including the world's largest collection of spread bird wings and the fifth-largest collection of Northwest Coast Native American art. Its $106 million Tom Kundig-designed building opened in 2019 with windows into the working collections.
burke-museum-of-natural-history-and-cult.descriptor: Natural history and culture museum on the UW campus

writtenFor.name: Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture

burritos-california-university-district.descriptor: Mexican burrito counter in the University District

cactus-alki-beach.text: Brothers Bret and Marc Chatalas opened the first Cactus in Madison Park in 1990, blending Southwestern, Mexican, Cuban and Spanish cooking — butternut squash enchiladas, brisket tacos, Dungeness crab tamales. Alki Point in West Seattle is one of the group's locations, serving that same menu out by Puget Sound.
cactus-alki-beach.descriptor: Southwest and Mexican plates at Alki Point in West Seattle

cactus-south-lake-union.text: Brothers Bret and Marc Chatalas opened the first Cactus in Madison Park in 1990, serving a mashup of Southwestern, Mexican, Cuban and Spanish food — butternut squash enchiladas, brisket tacos, tamales stuffed with ahi or Dungeness crab. The South Lake Union outpost sits in an Amazon-owned building, and in 2015 Cactus signed on to Amazon's Prime Now delivery service.
cactus-south-lake-union.descriptor: Southwestern-Mexican plates in South Lake Union; Seattle chain since 1990

cafe-allegro.text: Opened in 1975 in a 1909 building that had previously held shops, a bank and a funeral home, Allegro is Seattle's oldest coffeehouse and is credited as the city's first espresso bar — reached through an alley off University Way, across from the UW's main entrance. Founder Dave Olsen bought coffee by the pound from Starbucks and co-developed an espresso roast with them.
cafe-allegro.descriptor: U District alley coffeehouse, Seattle's first espresso bar, since 1975

cafe-campagne.text: Peter Lewis opened Café Campagne in 1994 at 1600 Post Alley as the casual, market-side little brother to his upstairs fine-dining room Campagne (1987–2011), evoking the cherished market-side cafés of France. Chef Daisley Gordon started at the original Campagne in 1995, cooked on Iron Chef America in 2008, and now owns the café, where the kitchen still makes its own sausages, charcuterie and duck confit.
cafe-campagne.descriptor: French bistro at 1600 Post Alley in Pike Place Market since 1994

cafe-flora.text: Open in Madison Valley since 1991, Cafe Flora is one of Seattle's longest-running vegetarian restaurants and has been at the forefront of local, organic sourcing built on direct relationships with Washington farms.
cafe-flora.descriptor: Vegetarian restaurant on E Madison St in Madison Valley since 1991

cafe-hagen.text: Danish-born Maria Beck opened the first Café Hagen in South Lake Union in December 2019, naming it for her hometown Copenhagen; the logo is a female warrior and one wall carries large black-and-white photos of women in custom-made armor. The counter runs to Scandinavian pastries, Danish cinnamon rolls and salmon toasts with Danish goat cheese, fennel and dill, plus coffee from Beck's own Hagen Coffee Roasters.
cafe-hagen.descriptor: Danish-inspired cafe and bakery on Thomas St in South Lake Union

cafe-hagen-slu.text: Cafe Hagen was started by Maria Beck, who settled in Seattle from Scandinavia and wanted to share hygge — "the cozy contentment and well-being you feel from enjoying the simple things in life." The original is in South Lake Union; pastries come from her family's Scandinavian recipes, and an exclusive coffee line is roasted only for Cafe Hagen.
cafe-hagen-slu.descriptor: Scandinavian cafe and bakery with its own exclusive coffee line

cafe-lago.text: Carla Leonardi opened Café Lago in Montlake in 1990, and the restaurant claims it produced Seattle's first wood-fired pizza. The bigger draw is the lasagne — the pasta is run through the machine three times for every layer — served alongside handmade gnocchi and Aunt Polly's meatballs.
cafe-lago.descriptor: Montlake trattoria since 1990, known for lasagne and wood-fired pizza

cafe-selam.text: Abebu Wondem opened Cafe Selam in 2002 — "selam" is Amharic for peace — and the injera is still made in house on a traditional two-day ferment, in regular and gluten-free teff versions. Her Ful Medames, a fava bean dish reflecting years in Sudan and Saudi Arabia, is a signature.
cafe-selam.descriptor: Ethiopian kitchen on E Cherry St in the Central District since 2002

cafe-turko.text: Gencer and Süreyya Gökeri founded the Turkish import business Istanbul Imports in 1991 before opening Café Turko in Fremont, and the dining room carries that over: Anatolian and Mediterranean decor, handmade Turkish rugs and an open kitchen. Süreyya is a trained teacher, cooking instructor and culinary-trip organizer.
cafe-turko.descriptor: Turkish restaurant and tea house on N 34th St in Fremont

caffe-darte.text: Caffé D'Arte was founded in Seattle by Mauro Cipolla, who apprenticed under a fourth-generation master roaster in Naples and built the company on traditional Italian craft. It roasts each single origin separately and blends afterward — its "post-blending" method — and pours the result at its Pioneer Square cafe on Yesler Way.
caffe-darte.descriptor: Italian espresso bar at 99 Yesler Way in Pioneer Square

caffe-ladro.text: Caffe Ladro started on Upper Queen Anne in 1994 and has grown to about 15 cafes around Seattle, adding its own roastery in 2011. "Ladro" is Italian for thief — the name was a cheeky jab at setting up as an alternative to the established coffee giant nearby.
caffe-ladro.descriptor: Local coffeehouse chain in Uptown near Seattle Center; roasts its own

caffe-umbria.text: Caffè Umbria was founded in 2002 in Georgetown by the Bizzarri family, third-generation Italian roasters, and opened this Pioneer Square flagship on Occidental Avenue in 2005 — a room described as one part Pioneer Square exposed brick, one part Perugia tile and ceramic, with an espresso machine imported from Italy.
caffe-umbria.descriptor: Italian espresso bar and roaster's flagship on Occidental Ave, Pioneer Square

caffe-vita.text: Mike McConnell started Caffe Vita in Queen Anne in 1995; the E Pike Street shop is the flagship, holding the cafe, the roastery and the company offices. He was an early champion of buying straight from growers — the "Farm Direct" model Vita still sources by.
caffe-vita.descriptor: Capitol Hill coffee roastery and cafe at 10th & Pike

caffe-vita-capitol-hill.text: Caffè Vita began in Queen Anne in 1995, when Mike McConnell became an early champion of buying green coffee straight from farmers — the "Farm Direct" model — well before that was standard practice; the roastery and flagship now sit on Capitol Hill. The W Galer St shop started life as a Caffe Fiore, and came into the Vita fold after Fiore's owner, Deming Maclise, took over the company in 2020.
caffe-vita-capitol-hill.descriptor: Queen Anne cafe of Seattle coffee roaster Caffè Vita, founded 1995

caffeumbria.text: Caffè Umbria is a Seattle coffee roaster started in 2002 by the Bizzarri family, third-generation Italian roasters whose flagship café opened in Pioneer Square in 2005. This Olive Way shop is one of four Seattle cafés pouring the company's Italian-style espresso.
caffeumbria.descriptor: Olive Way espresso bar downtown, from Seattle's Italian roaster Caffè Umbria

cal-anderson-park.text: The Lincoln Reservoir under the lawn was begun in 1889 after the Great Seattle Fire and finished in 1901, with the Olmsted Brothers designing the park around it. The site was renamed in 2003 for Cal Anderson, Washington's first openly gay state legislator, and in 2020 it sat at the center of the Capitol Hill Occupied Protest.
cal-anderson-park.descriptor: Capitol Hill park over the Lincoln Reservoir, with the Waterworks fountain

camp-long.text: Camp Long's Schurman Rock — a stone mound built by the Works Progress Administration between 1938 and 1939 and named for mountaineer and camp founder Clark Schurman, who wanted a safe artificial peak for beginners — is believed by some to be the first artificial climbing structure in the United States. The 68-acre West Seattle park around it was carved out of the West Seattle Golf Course and still rents rustic cabins overnight.
camp-long.descriptor: 68-acre West Seattle park with rustic cabins and a climbing rock

can-can-culinary-cabaret.text: A 120-seat dinner theater reached by a staircase down into Post Alley at Pike Place Market, Can Can pairs French-inspired Northwest plates built on Market farmers, butchers and fishmongers with original productions of burlesque, acrobatics, song and comedy. Its owners also bought and restored Portland's historic Paris Theatre, reopening it in November 2025.
can-can-culinary-cabaret.descriptor: Post Alley dinner-theater cabaret with burlesque and acrobatics

canlis.text: Peter Canlis opened it on December 11, 1950 in a Roland Terry-designed building that became an icon of Northwest-inspired modern architecture, and the same family still runs it. It's credited with inventing Northwest cuisine, and the Canlis Salad — romaine, bacon, romano, mint and oregano in a lemony Caesar-like dressing — has been on the menu since opening, often tossed tableside.
canlis.descriptor: Fine-dining landmark since 1950, above Lake Union

canon.text: Jamie Boudreau opened Canon on Capitol Hill in 2012 and stocked it with what the bar bills as America's largest spirits collection — 4,000 labels and counting, heavy on American whiskey. It placed sixth on Drinks International's World's 50 Best Bars in 2014, and the room is small enough that it only seats parties of four or fewer.
canon.descriptor: Whiskey and cocktail bar on 12th Ave with a 4,000-label spirits library

carl-s-english-jr-botanical-gardens.text: Botanist Carl S. English Jr. was hired by the Army Corps of Engineers in 1931 and spent 43 years of civil service turning the grounds of the Ballard Locks into an English-style landscape. The 17-acre garden now holds more than 500 species and roughly 1,500 varieties of plants, from fan palms and Mexican pines to an extensive fuchsia display.
carl-s-english-jr-botanical-gardens.descriptor: 17-acre garden on the Ballard Locks grounds, 500+ plant species

writtenFor.name: Carl S. English Jr. Botanical Gardens

carmelos.text: Carmelo Gaspar and Raul Delfin started Carmelo's Tacos in 2018 as a taco counter tucked inside Hillcrest Market on Capitol Hill, and the Mexico City-style al pastor and campechano built a following fast — The Daily Meal named it the best taco in Washington in 2020. It has since grown to three Seattle locations.
carmelos.descriptor: Mexico City-style taco spot on E Olive Way, Capitol Hill

carmelos-tacos.text: Carmelo Gaspar started the business in 2018 as a taco counter tucked inside Hillcrest Market on Capitol Hill, and it grew to three Seattle locations. The Mexico City-style tacos — al pastor, campechano with steak, chorizo and potato, and a vegan mushroom version with guajillo chile — got it named Washington's best taco by The Daily Meal in 2020.
carmelos-tacos.descriptor: Mexico City-style taco counter on Capitol Hill, started in 2018

cascina-spinasse.text: Spinasse opened in 2008 as a tiny rustic trattoria with communal seating and a hyper-focus on handmade pasta from Piedmont in northern Italy, and it has stayed on Seattle's best-Italian lists ever since. The dish to order is still the tajarin: fine hand-cut egg-yolk noodles with butter and sage. Chef Stuart Lane has run the kitchen since 2015.
cascina-spinasse.descriptor: Piedmontese pasta restaurant on 14th Ave, Capitol Hill, since 2008

cedars.text: Cedars occupies a converted house on Brooklyn Ave NE a few blocks off the UW campus, and has been a popular college hangout there for decades — a menu that runs from Indian curries and tandoori dishes to Mediterranean plates, with halal, vegetarian and vegan options and a long-running catering side business.
cedars.descriptor: Indian and Mediterranean kitchen in a converted house near the UW campus

center-for-wooden-boats.text: Founded in the 1970s by Dick Wagner on the south shore of Lake Union, CWB holds more than 170 vessels — mostly small sailboats and rowboats — and, unusually for a museum, lets you take them out. The livery fleet includes 20-foot Blanchard Junior Knockabouts designed and built at the Blanchard Boat Company on this same lake. Admission to the exhibits is always free, and the Sunday Public Sail puts visitors on the water.
center-for-wooden-boats.descriptor: Free maritime museum and boat livery on Lake Union Park's south shore

cha-cha-lounge.text: The Cha Cha opened on Cinco de Mayo 1998 alongside Bimbo's Bitchin' Burrito Kitchen, the E Pine taco shack where Capitol Hill musicians and artists made the burritos and poured the drinks. Development pushed both out, and in 2007 they reopened at 1013 E Pike — Bimbo's at street level, the Cha Cha in the basement below, all red light, velvet paintings and Mexican decor.
cha-cha-lounge.descriptor: Red-lit basement dive bar with Mexican kitsch on E Pike, Capitol Hill

changes.text: Changes Bar and Grill has billed itself as Wallingford's gay bar on its own website since at least the mid-2000s, and it runs on the neighborhood-bar basics rather than any signature dish: karaoke on Wednesdays and Sundays, Thursday trivia, all-day Thursday happy hour and a Sunday brunch.
changes.descriptor: Wallingford neighborhood gay bar on N 45th St with karaoke and bar food

cherry-street-coffee-house.text: Ali Ghambari's Cherry Street has been part of the Seattle brew scene since the late '90s, growing to seven cafes by late 2012 and eleven before the pandemic, which closed seven of them by May 2021. It's known less for a single roast than for an internationally influenced menu — Persian dishes at the First Avenue cafe, dirty chai, the caramel-mocha "Milkyway" — and a veggie burger with devotees among vegetarians and omnivores alike.
cherry-street-coffee-house.descriptor: Downtown 1st Ave cafe with an internationally influenced menu and veggie burger

writtenFor.name: Cherry Street Coffee House - Downtown (1st Avenue)

cherry-street-coffee-house-downtown-1st-.text: Ali Ghambari founded Cherry Street Coffee House in the late 1990s and grew it to seven Seattle shops by late 2012; one sits in the Medical Dental Building on Olive Way. It serves daily-baked pastries, bagels and Persian rice bowls, and its veggie burger has "quietly racked up legions of rabid devotees, both vegetarian and omnivore."
cherry-street-coffee-house-downtown-1st-.descriptor: Local coffee chain in the Medical Dental Building on Olive Way

writtenFor.name: Cherry Street Coffee House - Downtown (Olive Way)

chiangs-gourmet.descriptor: Sichuan and Taiwanese Chinese restaurant on Lake City Way NE

chihuly-garden-and-glass.text: It opened on May 21, 2012 on the former site of the Fun Forest amusement park, right at the foot of the Space Needle. The centerpiece is the Glasshouse, where a suspended sculpture roughly 100 feet long — one of Chihuly's largest — hangs beneath the glass roof; the building earned LEED silver certification.
chihuly-garden-and-glass.descriptor: Dale Chihuly glass exhibit at Seattle Center, open since 2012

chinatown-gate.text: Seattle's Historic Chinatown Gate is a 45-foot paifang — a traditional Chinese ceremonial gateway — built of steel and plaster over the west end of South King Street. Construction started in 2006 and the gate was unveiled in February 2008, marking the formal entrance to the Chinatown–International District.
chinatown-gate.descriptor: 45-foot Chinese paifang gate over the west end of S King St, unveiled 2008

chinooks-at-salmon-bay.text: Chinook's sits inside Fishermen's Terminal, the Port of Seattle dock that has been home port to the North Pacific fishing fleet since 1914 — you eat wild Alaska salmon, Dungeness crab and Anthony's clam chowder with the working boats tied up outside the window. It is part of the Anthony's family of Northwest seafood restaurants.
chinooks-at-salmon-bay.descriptor: Casual Northwest seafood house at Fishermen's Terminal on Salmon Bay

chop-suey.text: Pearl Jam filmed five "Riot Act" music videos here in September 2002 — "I Am Mine," "Save You," "Love Boat Captain," "Thumbing My Way" and "1/2 Full." The room has high ceilings and a ramshackle faux-Chinese motif, and it still books electronica, hip-hop and alt-rock alongside dance nights like Candi Pop.
chop-suey.descriptor: Capitol Hill music club and bar on E Madison St

chucks-hop-shop.text: Chuck Shin opened Chuck's Hop Shop after looking for a welcoming place where beer enthusiasts with families could drink a good beer — so it pairs 50 beers on tap and communal tables with a dedicated play area for kids and a rotating lineup of food trucks out front, from poke to New Orleans soul food.
chucks-hop-shop.descriptor: Craft beer bar with 50 taps and rotating food trucks on E Union St

clarence-s-hec-edmundson-pavilion.text: The Pavilion went up in nine months for $600,000 and opened in December 1927; it was renamed in 1948 for Clarence "Hec" Edmundson, a 1912 Olympian who coached Husky basketball for 27 seasons. It hosted the NCAA Final Four in 1949 and 1952, and a $40 million renovation in 1999–2000 removed 20 view-blocking pillars.
clarence-s-hec-edmundson-pavilion.descriptor: UW basketball arena on the Montlake campus, opened in 1927

climate-pledge-arena.text: The arena began life as the Washington State Pavilion for the 1962 Century 21 Exposition. In the 2018-2021 rebuild the landmark roof was detached from its 20 original concrete Y-columns and held on temporary supports while crews excavated and rebuilt the bowl beneath it. Amazon bought the naming rights in 2020 and named it for its climate pledge rather than itself; it reopened in October 2021.
climate-pledge-arena.descriptor: Kraken and Storm arena at Seattle Center under a 1962 World's Fair roof

cloudburst-brewing.text: Cloudburst brews out of a loading zone in a 120-year-old building just north of Pike Place Market, and its trophy shelf is outsized for its size: Great American Beer Festival Brewery of the Year in the 1,001–2,000 barrel class in 2021, a 2025 GABF silver for schwarzbier, and World Beer Cup golds for its rice lager and West Coast-style pilsner. A second, all-ages taproom sits in Old Ballard.
cloudburst-brewing.descriptor: Hop-forward brewery taproom on Western Ave just north of Pike Place Market

coba.text: Côba takes its name from the popular 2017 Vietnamese film "Cô Ba Sài Gòn," and the owners say the kitchen works from family recipes and techniques passed down through generations, plated as modern cuisine with a modern American twist.
coba.descriptor: Modern Vietnamese-American restaurant at 530 1st Ave N

college-inn-pub.text: The pub sat in the basement of the College Inn, one of Seattle's last remaining buildings from the 1909 Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition, and served the U District for more than 50 years. Legend says its Snug Room is haunted by a resident spirit the regulars call Howard the Ghost.
college-inn-pub.descriptor: Basement pub under the 1909 College Inn on University Way NE

comet-tavern.text: The Comet is Capitol Hill's best-known dive, long described as a grunge institution and a rocker's hangout on the Pike/Pine strip. Locals sent off the old room with a farewell party in early March 2014; it reopened after a renovation on March 31, 2014.
comet-tavern.descriptor: Capitol Hill dive bar at 922 E Pike St, a longtime rocker hangout

communion.text: Chef Kristi Brown — who started out washing dishes at a downtown Seattle café and ran That Brown Girl Catering from 1999 until 2009 — opened Communion with her son Damon Bomar in December 2020, on E Union Street in the Central District. The cooking is Southern-rooted and Pacific Northwest–inspired, and her lifelong mantra is "Everybody's Gotta Eat!"
communion.descriptor: Kristi Brown's Southern-rooted, Northwest-inspired restaurant in the Central District

conor-byrne.text: The pub traces its lineage back more than a century to its days as the Owl Saloon, and it books live music seven nights a week. In May 2024 a group of employees, musicians and community members bought it from the previous owners as the Conor Byrne Cooperative, which now counts more than 600 member-owners.
conor-byrne.descriptor: Ballard Ave music pub with live bands seven nights a week

cookies-country-chicken-west-woodland.text: Founder Brian Chandler spent a decade in the maritime industry as a chief steward, cooking for work crews in the South Louisiana oil fields, where he decided fried chicken was the one meal that brought everyone together. Cookie's ran as a pandemic-era pop-up before settling into permanent shops in Ballard and Pioneer Square.
cookies-country-chicken-west-woodland.descriptor: Fried chicken counter in Ballard — "fried chicken every way but fancy"

copacabana.text: Copacabana opened in the Sanitary Market in 1964 and moved to the 1910 Triangle Building in the late 1970s, and is described as one of the oldest Latino restaurants in Seattle. According to Fodor's, much of the strategy that saved Pike Place Market in the 1960s was hatched at this small Bolivian café, whose red-chaired deck still gets called one of the best views in the market.
copacabana.descriptor: Bolivian café with a Pike Place Market deck, open since 1964

copperworks-tasting-room-distillery.text: Copperworks makes American single malt the brewer's way: local breweries including Pike, Elysian and Fremont brew it a hop-free wort from locally grown barley, and Copperworks twice-distills that in copper stills handcrafted by the Scottish still maker Forsyths. Co-founder Jason Parker got his start brewing at Pike Brewing in 1989, and the distillery was named Distillery of the Year by the American Distilling Institute in 2018.
copperworks-tasting-room-distillery.descriptor: Waterfront single-malt whiskey distillery and tasting room on Alaskan Way

costas.text: Costa's opened on University Way in 1975 and has been serving traditional Greek dishes alongside American diner favorites ever since — breakfast through dinner, seven days a week, on a stretch of the Ave where most tenants turn over far faster.
costas.descriptor: Greek-American diner on the Ave (University Way NE) since 1975

crepe-de-france.text: A family crêperie that has operated inside Pike Place Market since 1991, making its crêpe recipes with the freshest ingredients purchased within the Market itself. The Market's directory gives the walking directions — head left from the fish throwers, stay right of the stairs — and points you at the crêpe au saumon, France and the Pacific Northwest on one plate.
crepe-de-france.descriptor: Sweet and savory crêperie inside Pike Place Market since 1991

cutters-crabhouse.descriptor: Waterfront seafood house near Pike Place with Elliott Bay views

cyclops.text: Cyclops sits in one of Belltown's few surviving early-1900s buildings, a former workers' hotel it moved into after its original home was demolished in 1997. The walls are a rotating gallery of friends' art and Seattle music memorabilia — a Jimi Hendrix pick, one of Krist Novoselic's teeth — and the Seattle Star reports Soundgarden, Eddie Vedder and Dave Grohl have all passed through.
cyclops.descriptor: Eclectic art-filled Belltown bar and café

damn-the-weather.descriptor: Cocktail bar and bar-food kitchen on 1st Ave S in Pioneer Square

daniels-broiler.text: Daniel's is the steakhouse arm of Schwartz Brothers Restaurants, the Seattle family company Bill and John Schwartz started with The Butcher in Bellevue in October 1970. The Lake Union room sits right on the water at 809 Fairview Place North, serving prime cuts under a view across the lake to Gas Works Park and the Queen Anne skyline.
daniels-broiler.descriptor: Lake Union waterfront prime steakhouse with Gas Works Park views

daniels-broiler-slu.text: The Schwartz Brothers restaurant group started with The Butcher, opened in Bellevue in October 1970, and grew into four Daniel's Broiler steakhouses; this one sits on the second floor of the Hyatt Regency Seattle at 808 Howell Street. Its Rickhouse Whiskey Bar is built around a 36-barrel bourbon display wall and pours more than 150 whiskeys and premium spirits.
daniels-broiler-slu.descriptor: Prime steakhouse in the Hyatt Regency on Howell St, with a big whiskey bar

daybreak-star-indian-cultural-center.text: Daybreak Star exists because of a protest. In 1970 Bernie Whitebear and roughly 100 Native activists and supporters staged a direct action at Fort Lawton, which the Defense Department had declared surplus property. After months of occupation, arrests and negotiations, United Indians of All Tribes secured a 99-year renewable lease on 20 acres in 1971, and the center opened in 1977. It still hosts powwows, a Head Start preschool and a Native art gallery.
daybreak-star-indian-cultural-center.descriptor: Native cultural center and gallery in Discovery Park, opened 1977

de-luxe-bar-grill.text: The DeLuxe opened as a tavern at the close of Prohibition, and the small grill added in back in the late 1950s got known for mammoth baked potatoes and cheap steak dinners. Joe Rogel and Bernie Minsk bought the place in the early 1960s; Joe's son Barry and his wife Keely took it over in 1999.
de-luxe-bar-grill.descriptor: Burgers and beer at Broadway & Roy, a tavern since the end of Prohibition

delancey.text: Delancey grew out of Molly Wizenberg's food blog Orangette: she and chef Brandon Pettit opened the wood-fired, Brooklyn-style pizzeria in Ballard in 2009 and added a pantry next door in 2011. The restaurant became the subject of Wizenberg's memoir "Delancey: A Man, A Woman, A Restaurant, A Marriage."
delancey.descriptor: Wood-fired Brooklyn-style pizzeria in Ballard, open since 2009

dicks-drive-in-broadway.text: Dick's second location opened on Capitol Hill in 1955, a year after the Wallingford original. Sir Mix-a-Lot name-checked this one in a 1988 track as a local hangout — and the menu still runs on well-done burgers, hand-cut fries, and individually made shakes.
dicks-drive-in-broadway.descriptor: Capitol Hill burger drive-in on Broadway since 1955

dicks-drive-in-queen-anne.text: Seattle's homegrown burger chain started in Wallingford in 1954; the Queen Anne shop, added in 1974, is the only Dick's with indoor tables and no drive-in. The menu has barely changed — Deluxes, hand-cut fries, individually made shakes — and the company is nearly as famous locally for fully employer-paid medical insurance and college tuition scholarships.
dicks-drive-in-queen-anne.descriptor: Burger stand in Queen Anne, open since 1974

dicks-drive-in-wallingford.text: The first Dick's opened here on January 28, 1954, and the formula has barely moved since: a short menu of well-done burgers, hand-cut fries, and individually made shakes, with no substitutions allowed. The chain is also known for paying unusually well for fast food — 100% employer-paid medical, a matched 401(k), and a tuition scholarship after six months on the job.
dicks-drive-in-wallingford.descriptor: The original Dick's Drive-In, on NE 45th St since 1954

diesel.text: Diesel opened in 2011 to serve Seattle's bear scene, and Thrillist has described its crowd as "bears, bikers, buddies, bubbas, blue collars, and bad asses." Bear World magazine put it on its 2019 list of the world's best bear bars.
diesel.descriptor: Gay bar serving Seattle's bear, leather and daddy scene in Capitol Hill

dinos-tomato-pie.text: Dino's is Brandon Pettit's Capitol Hill follow-up to his Ballard pizzeria Delancey — a mirrored, wood-boothed pizza bar announced in 2015 that serves square Sicilian/Jersey-style tomato pie, garlic knots and negronis. The signature Mr. Pink comes with vodka sauce, mozzarella, ricotta and basil.
dinos-tomato-pie.descriptor: Square Sicilian/Jersey-style pizza and cocktails on E Olive Way, Capitol Hill

discovery-park.text: At 534 acres it's Seattle's biggest park, and until the early 1970s it was Fort Lawton, a U.S. Army post; the surplus land was transferred to the city in 1972 and dedicated in 1973, named for HMS Discovery. Its Daybreak Star Cultural Center sits on 20 acres won after Native activists led by Bernie Whitebear occupied the base in 1970 and secured a 99-year lease. The West Point Lighthouse anchors the shoreline.
discovery-park.descriptor: Seattle's largest park — 534 acres of bluff, forest and beach in Magnolia

diva-espresso.text: Diva is a small independent Seattle coffeehouse chain — seven cafes, three of them on Greenwood Avenue N — that doesn't roast its own beans. It brews coffee from Highlands Coffee Company instead, established in North Seattle in 1992 as Diva's exclusive custom roaster.
diva-espresso.descriptor: Independent local coffeehouse on Greenwood Ave N at N 80th

dough-zone.text: Jason and Nancy Zhai opened the first Dough Zone in Bellevue in 2014 and grew it into a Chinese dumpling chain with locations across Washington, plus Portland, Beaverton and California. The Infatuation named it one of the 25 best restaurants in Seattle's Chinatown-International District in 2025.
dough-zone.descriptor: Chinese dumpling house from a chain born in Bellevue in 2014

dough-zone-downtown-5th-avenue-south.text: Dough Zone started in 2014 as a mom-and-pop shop in Bellevue and grew into a West Coast chain. Its signature is the Q-Bao, a pan-fried bun modeled on Shanghai's sheng jian bao with a soupy pork filling, served alongside xiao long bao and Sichuan dan dan noodles.
dough-zone-downtown-5th-avenue-south.descriptor: Soup dumplings and pan-fried Q-Bao, downtown Seattle

due-cucina-junction.text: Due' Cucina was started in Seattle in 2017 by Davide and Filippo, two high-school friends from Italy with a passion for pasta. Pasta, bread, sausage, dressings and desserts are all made in-house from scratch, and the kitchen promises fresh pasta in under eight minutes.
due-cucina-junction.descriptor: Fast-casual Italian restaurant serving house-made pasta from scratch

dukes-seafood.text: Duke Moscrip built this Puget Sound seafood chain on wild, sustainably caught salmon, Dungeness crab and prawns, four house chowders, and a standing promise from the founder: enjoy your meal or you don't pay. The Green Lake room at 7850 Green Lake Drive N has an outdoor patio with lake views, an easy stop after a lap around the loop.
dukes-seafood.descriptor: Seafood house on Green Lake Drive N with a lakeside patio and four chowders

dukes-seafood-chowder.text: Duke Moscrip's six-restaurant Puget Sound chain is built on wild, sustainably caught seafood and four house chowders. South Lake Union is the downtown location, billed by the company as some of the best waterfront-view dining in Seattle, and Moscrip still backs every plate with his line: enjoy your meal or you don't pay.
dukes-seafood-chowder.descriptor: Waterfront seafood spot in South Lake Union known for its chowders

duwamish.text: Built in 1909, the Duwamish fought fires for the Seattle Fire Department for 76 years before retiring in 1985. After a 1949 repowering its pumps pushed 22,800 gallons a minute, making it the most powerful fireboat in the world until 2003. It was named a National Historic Landmark in 1989 and is now moored at Lake Union Park beside MOHAI.
duwamish.descriptor: 1909 fireboat museum ship at Lake Union Park's Historic Ships Wharf

earls-on-the-ave.text: Earl's has been the University District's sports-bar default since 1989, one block off the UW campus: nine TVs plus a 12-foot projector screen, pool tables, stiff drinks and a kitchen that stays open until 2 a.m. It opens early on UW and Seahawks game days.
earls-on-the-ave.descriptor: No-nonsense sports bar on the Ave since 1989, kitchen open till 2 a.m.

eastlake-zoo-tavern.text: The Zoo opened in 1974 and is still a worn-green, deep-set neighborhood room. It packs in three pool tables, snooker, ping-pong, darts, shuffleboard, pinball, arcade games, foosball and Skee-Ball, runs an annual spring "Zoo Olympics" with local breweries, and keeps a worn 1977 Northwest Pool League city runner-up plaque on one of its wooden booths.
eastlake-zoo-tavern.descriptor: Eastlake tavern since 1974, packed with pool tables and games

el-camino.text: El Camino has been on N 35th St in Fremont since 1996, cooking southern Mexican food from Michoacán to Oaxaca out of chef Arturo Perez's family recipes, with menu input from Mexico City chef Ricardo Muñoz Zurita. Moles, salsas and desserts are made from scratch, and the covered, heated patio keeps the margaritas going year-round.
el-camino.descriptor: Southern Mexican cooking and margaritas in Fremont since 1996

el-camion.text: Scott McGinnis, who grew up on Mexican food in Southern California, parked his first El Camión truck in north Seattle around 2007; it grew into a small fleet — Ballard, Roosevelt, North Seattle and Sand Point — with the first sit-down location opening in Ballard in February 2013. The trucks' motto sums up the priorities: "¡Taco sin salsa no es taco!"
el-camion.descriptor: Taco truck on Roosevelt Way NE from Seattle's El Camión fleet

el-chupacabra.text: Open since 2005, El Chupacabra bills itself as "a punk rock cantina serving up delicious burritos and margaritas" — mission-style Mexican food, house-made hot sauces and salsas, and music played loud. The West Seattle room sits at 2620 Alki Ave SW near the beach; the other is at 6711 Greenwood Ave N.
el-chupacabra.descriptor: Punk-rock Mexican cantina on Alki Beach, burritos and margaritas since 2005

el-chupacabra-phinney-ridge.text: El Chupacabra has been slinging mission-style burritos, house-made hot sauces and margaritas from its Greenwood Avenue cantina since 2005, with a deliberately loud punk-rock look and a long list of vegetarian and vegan options. A second location sits on Alki Ave in West Seattle.
el-chupacabra-phinney-ridge.descriptor: Punk-rock cantina on Greenwood Ave N since 2005 - wet burritos, margaritas

el-gaucho.text: The original El Gaucho ran at 7th and Olive from 1953 to 1985; Paul Mackay, who had worked there, brought the name back in Belltown in 1996, keeping the old-school tableside service. The flagship moved into the Union Stables building in 2021.
el-gaucho.descriptor: Old-school Belltown steakhouse with tableside service, revived in 1996

el-moose.text: El Moose has cooked Mexican comida típica on Leary Ave NW in Ballard since 2004, from family recipes the owners say were handed down for decades and inspired by Mexican markets and roadside restaurants. It leans regional rather than Tex-Mex — carnitas street tacos, huevos divorciados and plantains with cinnamon sugar, with breakfast served every day.
el-moose.descriptor: Mexican comida típica on Leary Ave NW in Ballard since 2004

elliott-bay-brewery-and-pub.text: Todd Carden and Brent Norton opened Elliott Bay Brewing on California Ave SW in 1997, when Washington had only 33 breweries, and built it into the city's first certified organic brewing company. The brewery uses organic ingredients — a choice it says adds six to eight weeks to each batch and costs more.
elliott-bay-brewery-and-pub.descriptor: West Seattle brewpub on California Ave SW, brewing organic beer since 1997

emmett-watsons-oyster-bar.text: Seattle newspaper columnist Emmett Watson opened this oyster bar with his friend Sam Bryant on February 18, 1979, and it's billed as the city's first. It's still going in Pike Place Market, run now by Sam's son Thurman Bryant, and it sits on the James Beard Foundation's America's Classics list.
emmett-watsons-oyster-bar.descriptor: Pike Place Market oyster bar and seafood counter, open since 1979

espresso-vivace.text: David Schomer, a former Boeing engineer, and Geneva Sullivan started Vivace as a coffee cart at 5th and Union in 1988. Schomer is credited with developing and popularizing latte art in the United States, and since 1992 the shop has used a Northern Italian roast pushed to the peak of caramelized sugar — the reason it is known as "the caramel coffee."
espresso-vivace.descriptor: Capitol Hill flagship cafe of Seattle's latte-art pioneer, founded 1988

espresso-vivace-alley-24.text: Espresso Vivace was founded in 1988 by David Schomer, a former Boeing engineer, and Geneva Sullivan, a mainframe technician — and Schomer is credited with developing and popularizing latte art in the United States. Alley 24 is the roaster's South Lake Union café, one of just two Vivace locations left after the original Capitol Hill sidewalk bar closed in 2023.
espresso-vivace-alley-24.descriptor: South Lake Union café from the roaster that popularized US latte art

essential-baking-cafe.text: George DePasquale and Jeff Fairhall started The Essential Baking Company in 1994, selling artisan breads at Seattle's Fremont Farmers Market. They opened a bakery café in Wallingford in 1998 and later moved to Georgetown, where the bakery produces USDA Certified Organic artisan breads distributed across the Pacific Northwest.
essential-baking-cafe.descriptor: Café at Essential Baking's organic bakery in Georgetown

ezells-chicken.text: Ezell Stephens and Lewis Rudd opened the first Ezell's in Seattle's Central District, near Garfield High School, on February 3, 1984. Oprah Winfrey later called it her favorite fried chicken and is said to have it flown to her in Chicago when a craving hits — the endorsement behind the growth of a neighborhood shop into a regional chain.
ezells-chicken.descriptor: Fried chicken shop in Seattle's Central District, open since 1984

ezells-chicken-wallingford.text: Ezell Stephens and Lewis Rudd, both from Scottsville, Texas, opened the first Ezell's in 1984 on 23rd Avenue by Garfield High School, funded by an SBA loan and night-school business classes. Oprah Winfrey called it her favorite fried chicken and is said to have had it flown to Chicago when a craving hit; the Central District original is still the flagship.
ezells-chicken-wallingford.descriptor: Seattle fried-chicken institution on N 45th St; chain founded in 1984

fainting-goat-gelato.text: A family that moved to Seattle from Izmir, Turkey in 1997 opened Fainting Goat in Wallingford in 2009, calling it the small shop they'd dreamed of ever since; they run it with help from their three daughters. The gelato uses organic milk from Medosweet Farms and locally sourced seasonal fruit, on a rotating board that runs Sicilian pistachio, sea salt caramel, stracciatella and tiramisu.
fainting-goat-gelato.descriptor: Family-run organic gelato shop on N 45th St in Wallingford since 2009

fats-chicken-and-waffles.text: Marcus Lalario opened Fat's in September 2015 in the old Catfish Corner space at MLK Jr. Way and Cherry, and The Stranger named its fried chicken the best in Seattle in 2017. The 17-foot Martin Luther King Jr. portrait on the outside wall was painted by James Crespinel in 1995; after it was vandalized on MLK Day in 2022, the neighborhood raised $18,000 and Crespinel traveled from Mexico to repaint it.
fats-chicken-and-waffles.descriptor: Southern and soul food in the Central District at MLK Way and Cherry

fish-ladder-viewing-room.text: The original 1917 fish ladder at the Ballard Locks didn't work well, so the Army Corps rebuilt it in 1976 — going from 10 steps to 21 and adding an underground gallery where you can watch salmon push upstream through windows. Chinook, coho and sockeye all run here; peak viewing is roughly early July through mid-August. It's an unusual ladder in that it sits right where saltwater meets fresh.
fish-ladder-viewing-room.descriptor: Underwater salmon-viewing windows at the Ballard Locks fish ladder

flatstick-pub.text: Flatstick pours exclusively from breweries in Washington state and invented its own bar games — Duffleboard, Wickets and Pockets — that you can't play anywhere else. The South Lake Union location on Westlake Ave N adds a nine-hole indoor mini golf course and a darts room, plus brick-oven pizza.
flatstick-pub.descriptor: Mini golf, Duffleboard and Washington-only craft beer in South Lake Union

flatstick-pub-pioneer-square.text: This is the original Flatstick, which started as an underground putt-putt bar in Pioneer Square before the concept spread to Kirkland, South Lake Union, Redmond and Spokane. The nine-hole course spells out S-E-A-T-T-L-E through kegs and tunnels and finishes at a replica Space Needle, and the taps pour only Washington-made beer.
flatstick-pub-pioneer-square.descriptor: Indoor mini-golf pub with Washington-only taps on 2nd Ave S

fog-room.text: The Fog Room sits 16 stories above downtown at the Charter Hotel, two blocks from Pike Place Market, with a covered indoor-outdoor terrace looking over the skyline and Puget Sound. It's a fixture on rooftop-bar lists, having been named by Seattle Magazine, Thrillist and BuzzFeed.
fog-room.descriptor: Rooftop cocktail lounge and terrace 16 floors above 2nd Avenue downtown

fogon-cocina-mexicana.text: A 110-seat Capitol Hill restaurant that the Seattle Post-Intelligencer called the neighborhood's most popular Mexican spot, with bamboo tables and benches and a tortilla-making station. Seattle Met's verdict on the food: not terribly authentic, but "so cheap and tasty that nobody cares." Its sibling tequila bar, La Josie's, opened in 2020.
fogon-cocina-mexicana.descriptor: Mexican restaurant at 600 E Pine with a tortilla-making station

fort-lawton-historic-district.text: Fort Lawton opened in 1900 on Magnolia Bluff, on land that included 703 acres Seattle citizens and governments donated to the Army, and in WWII became the second-largest port of embarkation to the Pacific — more than a million troops passed through, and it held German and Italian POWs. In 1970 Native American activists led by Bernie Whitebear occupied the fort, winning the land that became Daybreak Star; the best-preserved early buildings were declared a landmark district in 1988.
fort-lawton-historic-district.descriptor: Old Army post buildings preserved inside Discovery Park on Magnolia Bluff

fort-st-george.text: Fort St. George hides upstairs on the second floor above South King Street in the Chinatown-International District, opening only in the evenings. The menu is izakaya drinking food plus Japanese takes on Western dishes — menchi katsu (deep-fried hamburger steak), chicken tempura, geso karaage, pork and kimchi hot pot.
fort-st-george.descriptor: Second-floor Japanese izakaya on S King St in the Chinatown-ID

frankie-jos-capitol-hill.text: Autumn Martin started Frankie & Jo's in 2013 and opened the first shop with co-founder Kari Brunson in 2016; there are now three in Seattle plus one in Larkspur, California. Everything is plant-based and made without gums, stabilizers or soy — flavors like beet strawberry rose and chocolate tahini supercookie, in waffle cones made from scratch with oat flour.
frankie-jos-capitol-hill.descriptor: Plant-based ice cream scoop shop on E Union St, Capitol Hill

freeway-park.text: Freeway Park opened on the Bicentennial — July 4, 1976 — built on a lid over Interstate 5, with 5.2 acres of blocky concrete canyons and waterfalls. Designed by Lawrence Halprin's office under Angela Danadjieva, its brutalist-meets-greenery design is now on the National Register of Historic Places (2019) and a designated Seattle Landmark (2022).
freeway-park.descriptor: Brutalist 5.2-acre park built on a lid over I-5, opened 1976

fremont-brewing-company.text: Founded in 2009 by Matt Lincecum and Sara Nelson, Fremont Brewing pours Universale Pale Ale, Interurban IPA and Abominable Winter Ale at its Fremont taproom, with hops from the Yakima Valley and water from the Cedar River watershed. It is now the third-largest craft brewery in Washington and the state's largest producer of barrel-aged beer.
fremont-brewing-company.descriptor: Fremont taproom behind Interurban IPA, brewing since 2009

fremont-brewing-urban-beer-garden.text: Matt Lincecum and Sara Nelson founded Fremont Brewing in 2009; it is now the third-largest craft brewery in Washington and the state's biggest producer of barrel-aged beer, behind Interurban IPA and Universale Pale Ale. Nelson later won a seat on the Seattle City Council and served as its president from 2024 to 2026. The Urban Beer Garden in Fremont is where it all pours.
fremont-brewing-urban-beer-garden.descriptor: Fremont taproom with a big outdoor beer garden, home of Interurban IPA

fremont-coffee-company.text: Fremont Coffee has poured since 2003 out of a rickety old house on N 36th Street, and the wraparound porch is half the reason people go — The Infatuation calls the eternally creaking space as iconic as the coffee. The shop roasts its own beans and hangs a rotating show of local art on the walls each month.
fremont-coffee-company.descriptor: Coffeehouse in an old Fremont house with a wraparound porch, open since 2003

frye-art-museum.text: Meatpacking magnate Charles Frye and his wife Emma left Seattle their 232-painting collection with strings attached: admission had to stay free, the works had to hang permanently in natural light, and abstract art was excluded. The museum opened on First Hill in 1952 and is still free, though after 2007 it began programming contemporary and conceptual art well beyond the founders' taste.
frye-art-museum.descriptor: Free First Hill art museum, open since 1952 by its founder's bequest

gas-works-park.text: The rusting towers are what's left of the coal gasification plant that cooked coal into gas here from 1906 to 1956. Rather than clear the site, landscape architect Richard Haag kept the machinery and opened the park in 1975 — a landmark of industrial reuse. The Great Mound is piled from plant rubble and topped with a sundial.
gas-works-park.descriptor: Lake Union park built on a 1906 coal-gas plant, with the Great Mound sundial

gates-foundation-discovery-center.text: The Gates Foundation opened this visitor center on Fifth Avenue N on February 4, 2012, and admission has always been free. Inside are interactive exhibits on malaria, education and homelessness, plus a "Find Your Skills" quiz that steers visitors toward real-world problems. The LEED Gold building used over 13,400 board feet of reclaimed ash and wall insulation made from recycled denim.
gates-foundation-discovery-center.descriptor: Free interactive exhibit hall at the Gates Foundation, open since 2012

gelatiamo.text: Maria Coassin opened Gelatiamo downtown at Third and Union in 1996. It has repeatedly been called the city's best gelato — Seattle Weekly said so in 2006, The Infatuation again in 2023 — and the same gelato turns up in the freezers at Pagliacci Pizza.
gelatiamo.descriptor: Italian gelateria at Third and Union downtown, open since 1996

general-porpoise-doughnuts-pioneer-squar.text: General Porpoise started on Capitol Hill and opened this Pioneer Square shop in March 2018. The whole point is filled doughnuts — vanilla, lemon, chocolate marshmallow, peanut butter and grape jelly. Thrillist singled out the lemon curd and put the shop on its list of the 32 best doughnut shops in America.

georgetown-brewing-company.text: Founded in 2002 by Manny Chao and Roger Bialous on a $200,000 stake, Georgetown got its start in the historic Seattle Brewing and Malting plant where Rainier Beer was once made. It built the business on draft beer alone: by 2011 Manny's Pale Ale was about 85% of sales and on tap in roughly 500 Seattle bars, and the brewery was at one point the largest draft-only operation in the country.
georgetown-brewing-company.descriptor: Georgetown brewery behind Manny's Pale Ale, founded 2002

ghostfish-brewing-company.text: Ghostfish brews nothing but gluten-free beer, built from unusual, naturally gluten-free grains rather than barley or wheat — the brewery's stated vision is to be North America's leading supplier of dedicated gluten-free beer. Flagships include Grapefruit IPA and Watchstander Stout, poured at the SoDo taproom and restaurant on 1st Ave S.
ghostfish-brewing-company.descriptor: Dedicated gluten-free brewery and taproom on 1st Ave S in SoDo

glos.text: Glo's opened on Capitol Hill in 1987 and built a reputation for exceptional breakfast in a tiny retro room — be prepared to wait — especially its eggs Benedict, the smoked salmon version above all, and late-night weekend hours (Time Out called it the best place to get a 3am omelette). A 2022 fire closed the original location indefinitely, and the business has since run pop-up brunches.
glos.descriptor: Tiny Capitol Hill breakfast spot known for eggs Benedict, since 1987

great-state-burger-downtown.text: Great State Burger is Josh Henderson's take on the plain old American burger joint — the founder of Skillet street food built it around pasture-raised, grass-fed beef, organic milkshakes made with Parfait ice cream and Theo chocolate, and a short menu, with the tagline "no gimmicks, just great burgers."
great-state-burger-downtown.descriptor: Fast-casual burger spot: grass-fed beef, organic shakes, locally sourced

green-lake-park.text: The lake was carved by the Vashon glacier and named by surveyor David Phillips in 1855 for the algae blooms it produced even in its natural state. It was folded into the Olmsted Brothers' Seattle park plan after 1903, and in 1911 the city lowered the water seven feet to create the shoreline parkland that now carries the 2.8-mile loop path.
green-lake-park.descriptor: Lakeside park in north Seattle with a 2.8-mile paved loop

hagen.text: Café Hagen opened in South Lake Union in 2019 as a Scandinavian take on the Seattle coffee shop, built on simplicity and attention to detail, with pastries baked at its own Freya Bakery and delivered to every café daily. It has since grown to seven locations around the region, and roasts its own coffee at the Uptown shop.
hagen.descriptor: Scandinavian-style café and coffee roastery on 5th Ave N in Uptown

hamdi.text: Hamdi began as a pop-up feeding brewery crowds Turkish kebaps in 2021 and opened its 50-seat Ballard room in November 2022. Owners Berk Güldal and Katrina Schult came out of Eleven Madison Park, The French Laundry and SingleThread; Esquire named it one of the 50 best new restaurants in America in 2023.
hamdi.descriptor: Turkish charcoal-grill restaurant on Leary Way in Ballard, kebaps and mezes

hatties-hat.text: Hattie's Hat has been a Ballard drinking establishment in one guise or another since 1904, with a stint as a fine dining establishment before settling back into divey bar-and-grill mode. It's known now for a famously beet-heavy comfort menu — a corned beef and beet "flannel" hash, Swedish pancakes — and a bloody-mary brunch under murals of natural scenery.
hatties-hat.descriptor: Ballard dive bar and grill, around in some guise since 1904

hello-robin.text: Robin Wehl Martin had built a Capitol Hill reputation for her baking when a text from Zack, husband of ice cream maker Molly Moon Neitzel, pushed her and her husband Clay from home baking into a storefront; Hello Robin opened in late 2013. The s'more cookie is the signature, and the shop now sells ice cream sandwiches and frozen bake-at-home dough too.
hello-robin.descriptor: Cookie shop on 19th Ave E in Capitol Hill's Miller Park, open since 2013

henry-art-gallery.text: The Henry opened in February 1927 as the first public art museum in Washington State, founded when Seattle businessman Horace C. Henry donated his 178-work collection and the money to build a home for it. Today it leans contemporary, and its best-known piece is permanent: James Turrell's 2003 Skyspace "Light Reign," a chamber with a retractable roof that frames the sky.
henry-art-gallery.descriptor: Contemporary art museum on the UW campus, Washington's first, from 1927

herkimer-coffee.text: Herkimer has roasted coffee in Seattle since 2003 and runs three cafes around the city; this Ravenna shop at 5611 University Way NE keeps short hours, 7am to 2pm daily.
herkimer-coffee.descriptor: Cafe on University Way NE from a Seattle roastery going since 2003

herkimer-coffee-phinney-ridge.text: Herkimer has roasted coffee in Seattle since 2003, and this Greenwood Avenue shop on Phinney Ridge is one of its three cafes; the others are in Ravenna and at 4th & Blanchard, and the roastery ships beans roasted the same day.
herkimer-coffee-phinney-ridge.descriptor: Independent coffee roaster and cafe on Greenwood Ave N since 2003

hilltop-ale-house.text: A 21-and-over neighborhood pub on Queen Anne that has served "splendid food and fine ales" since 1991, with a menu that runs past standard bar snacks to a habanero brisket burrito and an avocado-and-bacon turkey club on sourdough.
hilltop-ale-house.descriptor: Upper Queen Anne neighborhood pub serving food and ales since 1991

hing-hay-park.text: The park's Chinese name translates roughly as "Park for Pleasurable Gatherings." Its ornate pavilion was a gift from the mayor of Taipei, who paid out of his own funds for the pavilion and brickwork after learning Seattle couldn't cover the park's upkeep; it was completed in 1975. A 2017 expansion nearly doubled the park, and a 20-by-70-foot perforated red metal gateway was installed in early 2018.
hing-hay-park.descriptor: Chinatown-ID plaza with a Taipei-built pavilion and a red steel gateway

hiram-m-chittenden-locks.text: Opened in 1917, the Ballard Locks carry more boat traffic than any other lock in the United States, and the locks, fish ladder and botanical garden draw more than a million visitors a year. The fish ladder is unusual in sitting where salt water meets fresh. Building the ship canal lowered Lake Washington and Lake Union by about nine feet, permanently reshaping Seattle's shoreline.
hiram-m-chittenden-locks.descriptor: 1917 Ballard locks, fish ladder and gardens linking the Sound to Lake Union

holy-mountain-brewing.text: Holy Mountain grew out of a DIY homebrewing collective working in a former Alaska Copper Works warehouse on East Marginal Way, and opened its own brewery and taproom in 2014. It built its name on wood — naturally carbonated mixed-fermentation beers alongside lagers and hoppy styles — and calls itself Seattle's original oak- and barrel-focused brewery. The yeast culture from that first barrel-fermented beer is still in use.
holy-mountain-brewing.descriptor: Seattle taproom known for oak-aged and mixed-fermentation beer, since 2014

holy-mountain-brewing-taproom.text: The all-ages Phinney taproom of Holy Mountain Brewing, counterpart to the 21+ Interbay brewery whose name rests on wild yeast, oak and hops — saisons, barrel-aged beers and wild ales. The brewery frames its identity around art, music and mysticism, which is where the occult-leaning labels come from.
holy-mountain-brewing-taproom.descriptor: All-ages Phinney Ridge taproom of Holy Mountain Brewing, on Greenwood Ave N

homer.text: Logan and Sara Cox opened Homer in 2018 and named it after their golden retriever. The vegetable-forward, Middle East-meets-Northwest small plates made it Eater Seattle readers' Restaurant of the Year that first year, Seattle Met's Restaurant of the Year in 2019, and landed it on GQ's list of the best new restaurants in America.
homer.descriptor: Middle Eastern small plates on Beacon Hill since 2018

honey-court-seafood-restaurant.text: Honey Court is the Chinatown-International District's late-night dim sum answer: steamer baskets of prawn dumplings, pork buns and soy sauce rice rolls run until 3:30am on weekends, long after the rest of the neighborhood has gone dark.
honey-court-seafood-restaurant.descriptor: Cantonese seafood and dim sum on Maynard Ave S in the C-ID

honeyhole.text: Founded in 1999 on Capitol Hill's Pike Street, HoneyHole built its following on oddly named sandwiches — the Texas Tease, shredded barbecue chicken, and the Buford T. Justice, pork and pineapple — and won Seattle Magazine's 2018 readers' poll for best sandwich. It went dark in October 2023 when the general manager who had taken over that August disappeared, leaving staff unpaid; restaurateur Travis Rosenthal reopened the Capitol Hill shop in March 2024.
honeyhole.descriptor: Capitol Hill sandwich shop and bar on E Pike St, founded 1999

hood-famous-cafe-and-bar.text: Chera Amlag started Hood Famous in 2014, wholesaling ube (purple yam) cheesecakes to Uwajimaya; it grew into a 2016 Ballard storefront and then this 2019 Chinatown-International District cafe and bar. She co-owns it with her husband Geo Quibuyen of the hip-hop group Blue Scholars, and the menu runs from buko pie and cassava cake to arroz caldo, with calamansi sours and ube daiquiris at the bar.
hood-famous-cafe-and-bar.descriptor: Filipino cafe and bar in the CID known for ube cheesecake

hopvine-pub.text: The Hopvine bills itself as one of the only post-Prohibition taverns left on Capitol Hill: the space has held a tavern license since 1933, the year beer came back, and was fully renovated in 1995 into the beer-and-pizza neighborhood bar it is today. Rotating craft taps, hand-tossed pies, trivia nights and board games.
hopvine-pub.descriptor: Capitol Hill pub with rotating taps and hand-tossed pizza on 15th Ave E

hot-cakes.text: Hot Cakes started at Seattle farmers markets in 2008, selling raw cake batter in mason jars for people to bake at home. Four years of weekend markets later it opened a Ballard shop in 2012 and this Capitol Hill one, at 1650 E Olive Way, in 2015. The draw is still the Dark Decadence — the original 2008 molten chocolate cake, gooey in the middle, cakey outside.
hot-cakes.descriptor: Molten chocolate cake dessert bar on E Olive Way, Capitol Hill
