hot-cakes-capitol-hill.text: Autumn Martin's Hot Cakes started at Seattle farmers markets in 2008, selling raw frozen cake batter in mason jars for people to bake at home; this Ballard Ave shop followed in 2012, and a Capitol Hill location came in 2015. The Dark Decadence recipe has not changed since, and the spiked milkshakes — smoked chocolate with bourbon, mezcal with lime and caramel — drew national press.
hot-cakes-capitol-hill.descriptor: Molten chocolate cake shop on Ballard Ave NW, known for boozy shakes

hot-mamas-pizza.text: Hot Mama's has been turning out New York-style pizza on East Pine since 1995, selling by the slice as well as the whole pie — the Pesto and the House Combo are the house calls — with the ovens running to midnight on Friday and Saturday.
hot-mamas-pizza.descriptor: New York-style pizza by the slice on E Pine St, Capitol Hill, since 1995

how-to-cook-a-wolf-queen-anne.text: Ethan Stowell named this one after M.F.K. Fisher's 1942 book How to Cook a Wolf — a wartime-rationing cookbook about keeping the wolf from the door on very little — and the restaurant takes the same philosophy: simple ingredients transformed. The menu is handmade pasta and Pacific Northwest-inspired sharable plates.
how-to-cook-a-wolf-queen-anne.descriptor: Ethan Stowell pasta and shared plates on Queen Anne

writtenFor.name: How to Cook a Wolf - Queen Anne

hugo-house.text: Founded in 1997 and named for Seattle-born poet Richard Hugo, the literary center spent its first two decades in a 1902 Victorian that had previously housed a funeral home and New City Theater. That building was demolished in 2016 and Hugo House camped out on First Hill, then returned to the same Capitol Hill site in September 2018 inside a new six-story mixed-use building. It runs classes, readings and writer residencies.
hugo-house.descriptor: Capitol Hill literary center: writing classes, readings and open mics

hula-hula.text: Hula Hula has run what it calls tropical karaoke since 2006, pairing classic and contemporary tiki cocktails with cosmopolitan island kitsch and a mic that stays busy — karaoke starts at 7pm nightly. Local polls have handed it both Best Karaoke (Seattle Weekly) and Best Tiki Bar (KING 5).
hula-hula.descriptor: Tiki bar and karaoke joint on E Olive Way, Capitol Hill

husky-stadium.text: Open since November 1920, Husky Stadium holds the loudest crowd ever recorded at a college football stadium — ESPN clocked 133.6 decibels during Washington's 1992 game against Nebraska. It's also one of the very few stadiums fans reach by boat: as many as 12,000 people 'sailgate' on Lake Washington on game days. Its grandstand famously collapsed during construction in 1987, yet the project still finished on schedule.
husky-stadium.descriptor: UW football stadium on Lake Washington's Union Bay, open since 1920

i-love-sushi.text: The Seattle branch of a Bellevue family of Japanese restaurants that began with Shogun House on Main Street in 1981 — Bellevue's first Japanese restaurant — and opened the first I Love Sushi on NE 8th Street in 1986. This second location, overlooking South Lake Union, opened in 1992.
i-love-sushi.descriptor: Sushi restaurant overlooking South Lake Union, open since 1992

il-bistro.text: Il Bistro has served regional Italian food since 1975 from an intimate fine-dining room hidden beneath Pike Place Market, down a cobblestone alley toward the Market Theatre sign. Its cioppino is the long-standing order, and the dining room turns up on just about every list of Seattle's most romantic restaurants.
il-bistro.descriptor: Regional Italian fine dining down Post Alley at Pike Place, since 1975

il-terrazzo-carmine.text: Naples-born Carmine Smeraldo opened Il Terrazzo Carmine in Pioneer Square in 1984, and it became one of the city's go-to Italian rooms for celebrations and special occasions. Smeraldo has since died, but his line — "We don't have customers, we have family" — is still the house creed, and the family's group now also runs Intermezzo and a Carmine's in Bellevue.
il-terrazzo-carmine.descriptor: Old-school Italian fine dining in Pioneer Square since 1984

international-fountain.text: Built for the 1962 Century 21 World's Fair from a competition design by Tokyo architects Kazuyuki Matsushita and Hideki Shimizu, who beat out 260 other entries. WET Design rebuilt it in 1995 as a stainless steel dome with the jets set nearly flush so people can run right up to it — its four "super shooters" throw water as high as 120 feet, choreographed to music.
international-fountain.descriptor: Interactive musical fountain at Seattle Center, built for the 1962 World's Fair

ivars-acres-of-clams.text: Folk singer Ivar Haglund opened Seattle's first aquarium, with a fish-and-chips bar attached, on Pier 54 in 1938; the food outlasted the fish tanks, and Acres of Clams opened on the same spot on July 22, 1946. Haglund built the brand on stunts and the slogan "Keep Clam" — in 2009 the company staged a hoax about vintage billboards supposedly sunk in Puget Sound.
ivars-acres-of-clams.descriptor: Pier 54 seafood restaurant and chowder bar on the waterfront since 1946

ivars-fish-bar.text: Folk singer Ivar Haglund opened Seattle's first aquarium on Pier 54 in 1938 and tacked on a fish-and-chips bar to feed the visitors. The aquarium proved short-lived and closed about a decade later, but the fish bar and the clam chowder outlasted it — Haglund reopened the spot as Ivar's Acres of Clams on the same pier in 1946.
ivars-fish-bar.descriptor: Walk-up fish-and-chips and chowder counter on Pier 54

ivars-salmon-house.text: Ivar Haglund opened the Salmon House on Lake Union in 1971, built in the style of a Northwest Native longhouse. A large carved Welcoming Man greets diners, the kitchen grills wild salmon over alder, and the downtown skyline sits across the water.
ivars-salmon-house.descriptor: Alder-grilled salmon in a longhouse-style building on Lake Union

jacks-bbq.text: Jack Timmons grew up in Texas, moved to Seattle, and got serious enough about barbecue to attend Texas A&M's meat-science BBQ summer camp and tour the Central Texas pits before running a Seattle brisket pop-up and opening this SODO flagship in 2014. He hauls in Texas post oak, mesquite and hickory to smoke everything low and slow.
jacks-bbq.descriptor: Central Texas barbecue in SODO since 2014, smoked over Texas post oak

jacks-bbq-industrial-district.text: Founder Jack Timmons is a Texan who moved to Seattle, then went back to school for barbecue — BBQ Summer Camp at Texas A&M's Meat Science department in 2012 — before running a pop-up called the Seattle Brisket Experience and opening the original in SoDo. He still has post oak, mesquite and hickory trucked up from Texas for the pits, and this South Lake Union outpost runs the same smokehouse menu.
jacks-bbq-industrial-district.descriptor: Central Texas barbecue in South Lake Union, smoked over Texas hardwoods

jade-garden-restaurant.text: A Chinatown-International District dim sum standby that keeps landing on best-of lists for its overstuffed potstickers, honey BBQ pork hand pies and seared turnip cakes. The rolling carts are gone — you order electronically now. The dining room was remodeled around 2019, and the restaurant was vandalized in 2020 during the pandemic.
jade-garden-restaurant.descriptor: Cantonese dim sum house on 7th Ave S in the Chinatown-International District

jai-thai-fremont.descriptor: Family-style Thai kitchen at 3423 Fremont Ave N

jaks-grill.text: JaK's Grill is West Seattle's neighborhood steakhouse, with a second location in Issaquah. In 2025 it left its longtime California Ave SW home for the old Lodge space at 4209 SW Alaska in the Junction, adding 25–30 seats, a cherry-top bar and more beef cuts and shareable plates.
jaks-grill.descriptor: West Seattle Junction steakhouse, with a second location in Issaquah

japanese-garden.text: Dedicated in June 1960 at the south end of the Washington Park Arboretum, the 3.5-acre garden was designed by a Tokyo-selected team led by Kiyoshi Inoshita and landscape architect Juki Iida, using some 600 tons of granite boulders hauled down from Bandera Mountain near Snoqualmie Pass. The teahouse was a gift from the Tokyo government, shipped over in pieces in 1959; after a 1973 fire destroyed it, it was rebuilt in 1980–81 as Shoseian.
japanese-garden.descriptor: 3.5-acre Japanese stroll garden in the Washington Park Arboretum, from 1960

japonessa.text: Japonessa runs Japanese cooking fundamentals through Latin American flavors, so jalapeño, cilantro and mango show up alongside the nigiri and sashimi. It sits on 1st Ave a block from Pike Place Market, and is a downtown happy-hour standby.
japonessa.descriptor: Japanese-Latin sushi bar on 1st Ave near Pike Place Market

jefferson-park.text: Jefferson Park was laid out on Beacon Hill in 1908 as part of the Olmsted Brothers' plan for Seattle's park system, and the 18-hole golf course they designed opened in 1915. It is Fred Couples' home course; during World War II the park held anti-aircraft batteries and an Army recreation center with a gym and tent housing.
jefferson-park.descriptor: 52-acre Beacon Hill park with an Olmsted-designed municipal golf course

jimi-hendrix-park.text: A 2.3-acre park in the Central District, next to the Northwest African American Museum, honoring the Seattle-born guitarist. The site was named for Hendrix in 2006 but took until June 17, 2017 to open, with a guitar-shaped system of paths and plantings; the Bellevue School of Rock played a Hendrix tune at the ribbon-cutting. Backers included Hendrix's stepsister Janie and the Nisqually Tribe.
jimi-hendrix-park.descriptor: Central District park honoring Seattle-born Jimi Hendrix, opened 2017

jose-rizal-bridge.text: Built in 1911 as one of the first permanent steel bridges in Seattle, this steel arch carries 12th Avenue South from the International District up to Beacon Hill over South Dearborn Street and I-90, and was long known as the 12th Avenue South Bridge. It was renamed in 1974 for José Rizal, the Filipino national hero, and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1982.
jose-rizal-bridge.descriptor: 1911 steel arch bridge carrying 12th Ave S over Dearborn St and I-90

joule.text: Married chefs Rachel Yang and Seif Chirchi opened Joule in 2007 and moved it to Stone Way in 2012, running it as a self-described modern-day Korean steakhouse that has earned a James Beard nomination. The kalbi short rib — marinated in sake, mirin, pureed Asian pear, garlic and soy — is the dish people come for.
joule.descriptor: Korean fusion steakhouse on Stone Way in Wallingford, known for its kalbi

julias.text: Julia's on Broadway is best known as the home of Le Faux, the drag revue that bills itself as "Seattle's Drag Theatre Since 2000." Its shows and drag brunches keep the Capitol Hill room busy year-round.
julias.descriptor: Broadway bar and restaurant, home of the Le Faux drag show

julias-of-wallingford.text: Julia's has been at 4401 Wallingford Ave N since 1983, opening at 7am for a menu that pairs American brunch standards with Mexican breakfast dishes. It is now under new ownership but kept the name and the format.
julias-of-wallingford.descriptor: Wallingford brunch house since 1983; American plus Mexican breakfast

kamonegi.text: Chef Mutsuko Soma opened Kamonegi in Fremont in October 2017 after completing a two-year soba-making program in Japan; she's described as the only chef on the West Coast who rolls soba by hand. She was a James Beard finalist for Best Chef: Northwest and Pacific in 2022, and the restaurant was Seattle Metropolitan's 2018 Restaurant of the Year.
kamonegi.descriptor: Fremont soba house with hand-rolled buckwheat noodles and tempura

katsu-burger.text: Hajime Sato opened the first Katsu Burger in Georgetown in 2011, putting panko-breaded, deep-fried katsu patties on burger buns with Japanese flavors and curry- and nori-seasoned fries alongside. That original closed in 2014 and was bought and reopened the same year by Tom Jung and Stephanie Kang, who grew it into a regional chain; the Capitol Hill shop opened in 2017 and is the one with a bar.
katsu-burger.descriptor: Japanese panko-katsu burgers on 12th Ave, Capitol Hill

kau-kau-barbecue.text: Kau Kau has been roasting Cantonese barbecue in the Chinatown-International District since 1974, and the ducks and slabs of char siu hanging in the window are a neighborhood landmark. After running it for 50 years, Hock Wo handed the restaurant to his son Randy Wo-Eng in April 2024, with the stated aim of keeping it going another 50.
kau-kau-barbecue.descriptor: Cantonese BBQ on S King St since 1974, known for its char siu roast pork

kedai-makan.text: Kedai Makan started as a pop-up and then a tiny Olive Way takeout spot before growing into a full-service restaurant in 2015. Eater Seattle put it on its 2014 list of the city's 38 essential restaurants, and The Stranger praised the owners' "affection for and study of Malaysian food." It closed in October 2022 and reopened under new ownership, adding a Belltown location in May 2025.
kedai-makan.descriptor: Malaysian on E Pine, Capitol Hill — nasi lemak and sarawak laksa, since 2013

kells-irish-restaurant-bar.text: The McAleese family opened Kells in 1983 in the Butterworth Building, Seattle's first purpose-built mortuary — a 1903 funeral house whose elevator, the first on the West Coast, was installed to move bodies. The building's haunted reputation earned it a Ghost Adventures episode in 2010; Kells answers with live music from local talent every weekend.
kells-irish-restaurant-bar.descriptor: Irish pub near Pike Place Market, McAleese family-run since 1983

kerry-park.text: Lumberman Albert S. Kerry and his wife Katharine gave the city this 1.26-acre hillside in 1927 'so that all who stop here may enjoy this view' — the postcard shot of the Space Needle with Mount Rainier behind it. Doris Totten Chase's 15-foot steel sculpture Changing Form has framed photos here since 1971. It's the view used for Frasier's apartment and the opening of 10 Things I Hate About You.
kerry-park.descriptor: Queen Anne Hill viewpoint with the classic Space Needle skyline view

kings-hardware.text: A dimly lit Ballard Avenue hangout known for its two skee-ball machines and taxidermy, huge baskets of buffalo wings, and boozy slushies in rotating flavors.
kings-hardware.descriptor: Dim Ballard Avenue bar with skee-ball and taxidermy on the walls

kisaku-sushi.descriptor: Upscale sushi bar on N 55th St in Wallingford, near Green Lake

kite-hill.text: The hill is artificial: thousands of cubic yards of rubble from the old gas plant's building foundations, capped with fresh topsoil for the park that opened in 1975. At the top sits a sundial by local artists Chuck Greening and Kim Lazare that uses the visitor's own body as the gnomon — you stand on it and your shadow tells the time.
kite-hill.descriptor: Grassy mound at Gas Works Park with Lake Union and skyline views

klondike-gold-rush-national-historical-p.text: When the steamship Portland docked in Seattle in July 1897 loaded with Klondike gold, the news set off a stampede — and Seattle, pushed hard by newspaperman Erastus Brainerd's publicity campaign, made itself the outfitting capital for prospectors heading north. The mayor quit to start a transport company; a dozen cops and much of the streetcar crew walked off too. This free NPS visitor center in Pioneer Square tells that story.
klondike-gold-rush-national-historical-p.descriptor: Free NPS museum in Pioneer Square on Seattle's 1897 gold-rush boom

writtenFor.name: Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park

kobuta-and-ookami.text: The name means piglet and wolf — a nod to the Three Little Pigs — and the room is modeled on the cramped sake alleys tucked under Japan's elevated train tracks, which is what the owners set out to recreate. It's a family-owned katsu-and-sake house on 15th Ave E, with a second location in Redmond.
kobuta-and-ookami.descriptor: Family-run Japanese katsu and sake spot on 15th Ave E, Capitol Hill

kwanjai-thai.text: Kwanjai Thai is run by its namesake, who came to Seattle from Khon Kaen in northeastern Thailand intending to open a restaurant, and staffs the kitchen with her own family from Thailand. It has been feeding Fremont for well over a decade from a storefront on N 36th between Rudy's Barbershop and Fremont Coffee Company.
kwanjai-thai.descriptor: Longtime family-run Thai kitchen on N 36th St in Fremont

la-carta-de-oaxaca.text: Open in Ballard since 2003, La Carta de Oaxaca serves Oaxacan cooking — mole negro over pork ribs, tlayudas with chorizo and carne asada, lamb birria — alongside a deep mezcal and tequila list. Chef Gloria Perez is regarded as a matriarch of Oaxacan cuisine here; the family also runs El Mezcalito on Queen Anne.
la-carta-de-oaxaca.descriptor: Oaxacan restaurant in Ballard known for mole negro, since 2003

la-rustica.text: La Rustica has served Italian food on Beach Drive since 1996. When the previous owners retired, longtime regulars the Hoffmans - customers since 2002 - bought it in November 2020 and kept the menu, kitchen staff and service; the West Seattle Blog counted only four changes, one of them a house-made chocolate mousse cake. A September 2007 kitchen fire closed it for about ten days.
la-rustica.descriptor: Italian restaurant on Beach Dr SW in West Seattle, open since 1996

la-vita-e-bella.text: La Vita é Bella is a family-owned Italian restaurant on 2nd Avenue in Belltown, built around Sicilian roots — seafood dishes, house-made pasta and sauces, and thin-crust pizzas. There is a heated patio out front, and the kitchen buys produce from area farmers' markets.
la-vita-e-bella.descriptor: Family-owned Italian spot on 2nd Ave in Belltown, Sicilian specialties

lake-union-park.text: The 12-acre park at the south end of Lake Union opened in 2010 on ground the city spent years assembling — the last 5 acres came from the U.S. Navy in 2000. It's Seattle's maritime-history corner: MOHAI occupies the former Naval Reserve Armory, the Center for Wooden Boats sits alongside, and historic vessels including the tug Arthur Foss and the fireboat Duwamish tie up at the wharf.
lake-union-park.descriptor: 12-acre waterfront park at the south end of Lake Union, opened 2010

langston-hughes-performing-arts-center.text: The building opened in 1915 as a synagogue for the Orthodox congregation Chevra Bikur Cholim, a Byzantine Revival design by architect B. Marcus Priteca. The congregation sold it to the City of Seattle in 1969, and after renovation it reopened as a performing arts center devoted to Black and African American art, artists and audiences. It's a designated Seattle landmark.
langston-hughes-performing-arts-center.descriptor: Central District theater inside a 1915 Byzantine Revival former synagogue

large-lock.text: The large lock measures 80 by 825 feet and can raise a vessel about 26 feet from saltwater Puget Sound to the fresh water of the ship canal in roughly 10 to 15 minutes. The locks opened to traffic on May 8, 1917 — the first ship had passed through on August 3, 1916 — and they still carry more boat traffic than any other lock in the United States.
large-lock.descriptor: The 825-foot main chamber of the Ballard Locks, open since 1917

lark.text: Chef John Sundstrom opened Lark in 2003 and moved it to its E Seneca Street space in December 2014, where a four-course menu changes every month around the best seasonal products available. Sundstrom is a James Beard Award winner, the new room took Restaurant Design of the Year at the 2015 Seattle Design Awards, and Lark was a 2023 James Beard semifinalist for Outstanding Hospitality.
lark.descriptor: Four-course seasonal New American dining on E Seneca St, First Hill; open since 2003

latona-pub.text: The Latona has stood on Latona Ave NE near Green Lake since 1987 and has backed local independent brewers since the day it opened, with local musicians playing its small room. The kitchen cooks everything from scratch with Northwest purveyors and turns the menu over with the seasons.
latona-pub.descriptor: Green Lake craft beer pub with live music, pouring since 1987

le-fournil.text: Le Fournil has been turning out baguettes, croissants, quiches and macarons on Eastlake Avenue since 1997. The Stranger's listings site EverOut is blunt about it: "one of the best bakeries in town."
le-fournil.descriptor: French bakery and café on Eastlake Ave E, baking croissants since 1997

le-pichet.text: Le Pichet has served French café food on First Avenue beside Pike Place Market since August 2000, with slate tables, a rolled-zinc bar and a menu written almost entirely in French. Chef Jim Drohman is known for the roast chicken and the charcuterie plates, and Anthony Bourdain regularly recommended the place on his Seattle visits.
le-pichet.descriptor: French bistro on First Ave by Pike Place Market, open since 2000

leif-erikson-statue.text: August Werner's bronze Leif Erikson was unveiled during the 1962 World's Fair and now stands at Shilshole Bay Marina, where a 2007 project by artist Jay Haavik set it on a granite base ringed by a plaza of runic-carved stones arranged in the form of a Viking ship. The stones carry the names of Scandinavian immigrants and their descendants — 2,411 of them by 2014.
leif-erikson-statue.descriptor: Viking explorer statue at Shilshole Bay Marina in Ballard

lenox.text: Chef-owner Jhonny Reyes was born in Harlem and raised in Seattle; he started Lenox during the pandemic as a meal-delivery service, grew it into a pop-up, and then into this Belltown dining room. The food traces Puerto Rico, Cuba and Harlem, but as an interpretation rather than a replica — island flavors rebuilt with Pacific Northwest ingredients.
lenox.descriptor: Afro-Latin restaurant on 1st Ave in Belltown from chef Jhonny Reyes

life-on-mars.text: Life on Mars opened in June 2019 in Capitol Hill's Pike Flats building as a vegan bar and restaurant wrapped around a record shop, and has been described as a vinyl-record-themed bar. The kitchen sends out jackfruit tacos and cauliflower wings, and Reuben's Brews makes a custom IPA for it. Thrillist put it on its 2022 list of Seattle's best bars.
life-on-mars.descriptor: Vegan bar, kitchen and record shop on E Pike in Capitol Hill

lighthouse-roasters.text: Lighthouse has been roasting in Fremont since 1993, working small batches six days a week at its 400 N 43rd St shop and shipping orders placed before 9am the same day. The house style deliberately skips trend-chasing in favor of heavy body, dark chocolate and toffee sweetness.
lighthouse-roasters.descriptor: Fremont neighborhood roaster-cafe on N 43rd, roasting since 1993

lil-woodys.text: Marcus Lalario opened the first Lil Woody's on Capitol Hill in 2011, and it has since spread to Ballard, White Center, Green Lake, T-Mobile Park and Sea-Tac. Reader's Digest named it Washington's best burger in 2022 and 2023, and every February the shop runs a collaboration burger with a guest Seattle chef.
lil-woodys.descriptor: Burgers and shakes on Capitol Hill; the chain's original 2011 location

lil-woodys-capitol-hill.text: Marcus Lalario opened the first Lil Woody's at 1211 Pine Street on Capitol Hill in 2011; this one is the Ballard shop on NW Market St. Every February the burger counter hands its menu to guest chefs — J. Kenji Lopez-Alt, Canlis, Cafe Campagne and Spice Waala have all done a run — and the chain now has stands at T-Mobile Park, Sea-Tac and Climate Pledge Arena.
lil-woodys-capitol-hill.descriptor: Griddled burgers and shakes on NW Market St in Ballard

lindas-tavern.text: Opened in February 1994, Linda's became the "grunge Cheers" — the Capitol Hill living room of Seattle's music scene. It is also known for a grim piece of local trivia: it was the last place Kurt Cobain was spotted before his death that April.
lindas-tavern.descriptor: Capitol Hill dive bar on E Pine since 1994, with weekend brunch

little-red-hen.text: The Little Red Hen is Green Lake's country-western bar. Stone Temple Pilots filmed part of the 1993 video for "Plush" here, with the rest shot at an amusement park in Federal Way, south of the city.
little-red-hen.descriptor: Country-western bar in the Green Lake area of Seattle

lockspot-cafe.text: The Lockspot has been serving next to the Ballard Locks for roughly 90 years, and has turned up on Discovery's Deadliest Catch. Alison Soike and Ryan Faniel bought it from longtime owner Pam Hanson in 2021, saying they'd keep the old place's legacy intact.
lockspot-cafe.descriptor: Old-school cafe and bar on Locks Place, by the Ballard Locks entrance

lola.text: Tom Douglas opened Lola in July 2004 on 4th Avenue downtown. The Greek-influenced menu is a family tribute — the restaurant is named for co-owner Jackie's grandparents, Lola and Louie, and their photographs hang on the wall inside.
lola.descriptor: Tom Douglas's Greek-influenced restaurant on 4th Avenue downtown

lost-lake-cafe-lounge.text: Lost Lake opened in 2013 in a 3,000-square-foot space kitted out in '60s-era faux wood paneling and vintage chandeliers, and made its name as a 24-hour Capitol Hill diner with all-day breakfast — benedicts, fried chicken and biscuits, vegan hash. It came from the Guild Seattle group behind other Pike/Pine nightlife, and now closes overnight rather than running around the clock.
lost-lake-cafe-lounge.descriptor: All-day diner and cocktail lounge on 10th Ave, Capitol Hill, since 2013

loursin.text: L'Oursin — French for "sea urchin" — pairs modern takes on French classics like steak frites, raw scallops and fried sweetbreads with minimal-intervention natural wines. Chef J.J. Proville runs the kitchen, and there is a retail wine selection and wine club attached.
loursin.descriptor: French seafood and natural-wine spot on E Jefferson in the Central District

lowells.text: Lowell's has carried its name in Pike Place Market since 1957, in a space that earlier housed a combination coffee roaster, peanut roaster and cafeteria and then a Manning's. You order at the counter on the first and third floors and eat looking out at Elliott Bay, the port and the Olympics; the three-story restaurant turned up in Sleepless in Seattle.
lowells.descriptor: Three-story seafood diner in Pike Place Market with Elliott Bay views

ltd-edition-sushi.text: A small sushi counter on Nagle Place in Capitol Hill that opened in July 2021 and caps itself at about 30 omakase orders a day so the fish stays at its best. Within two years the New York Times put it on its 2023 list of the 50 best restaurants in America.
ltd-edition-sushi.descriptor: Omakase sushi counter on Nagle Place, Capitol Hill

ludis.text: A downtown Filipino diner that has been feeding Seattle in one location or another since the 1930s — it sat on the 200 block of Pike before moving to Stewart Street. Ludi's lost its lease and closed in 2019, then quietly reopened four years later in 2023.
ludis.descriptor: Filipino diner at 2nd & Stewart downtown, serving since the 1930s

lumen-field.text: Paul Allen pushed for an open-air bowl modeled on Husky Stadium, and the roof overhangs funnel crowd noise back down onto the field — Seahawks fans twice set the Guinness record for stadium loudness in 2013, first at 131.9 decibels and then at 136.6 later in the same game. The franchise retired the number 12 for its fans in 1984, and the 12 flag has been raised from a pole on the stadium rim since 2003.
lumen-field.descriptor: Open-air stadium in SoDo, home of the Seahawks and Sounders

luna-park-cafe.text: It's named for Luna Park, the 1907–1913 amusement park built on pilings off Duwamish Head and billed as "the greatest amusement park on the West Coast." The cafe opened in March 1989 in a building that had been a neighborhood tavern — Pat & Ron's Tavern until 1988 — and fills the room with vintage signs, knick-knacks and a working Seeburg jukebox.
luna-park-cafe.descriptor: Retro diner on SW Avalon Way in West Seattle, open since 1989

macrina-bakery-aloha.text: Leslie Mackie founded Macrina in Belltown in 1993, and it grew into a small chain of Seattle bakery cafés known for almond croissants, ginger cookies and dark-chocolate brownies. This is the SODO café on First Avenue South.
macrina-bakery-aloha.descriptor: SODO café of the Seattle bakery Leslie Mackie founded in 1993

macrina-bakery-belltown.text: Leslie Mackie opened Macrina in Belltown in 1993, and this shop is the original. It grew into a Seattle bread institution — Condé Nast Traveler named it a destination bakery in 2014 for its caramel turtle brownies — and the company now bakes out of a Kent headquarters and supplies stores around the region.
macrina-bakery-belltown.descriptor: Artisan bakery and café, Macrina's original Belltown shop since 1993

macrina-bakery-sodo.text: Leslie Mackie opened the first Macrina in Belltown in 1993, and it grew into one of Seattle's defining bread bakeries; the Aloha cafe, at 19th Ave E and E Aloha, was the fifth to open, on September 6, 2018. Condé Nast Traveler put Macrina on its 2014 list of 13 destination bakeries in America, singling out the caramel turtle brownies.
macrina-bakery-sodo.descriptor: Macrina's cafe at 19th Ave E and E Aloha — artisan breads and pastries

madison-pub.text: Chet Harold opened the pub in May 1986 and it became a gay bar that July. It has long sponsored local softball, rugby, basketball and volleyball teams, and The Stranger once described it as "the friendliest and least stressful gay bar on all of Capitol Hill."
madison-pub.descriptor: Gay sports bar on E Madison in Capitol Hill with darts, pool and pinball

maggie-bluffs.text: Maggie Bluffs sits at Elliott Bay Marina, the 1,200-slip Magnolia marina that opened in 1991 after 17 years in the planning and permit process. Its white-tablecloth neighbor Palisade, at 2601 W Marina Place, was run by Restaurants Unlimited until Houston-based Landry's picked it up out of the 2019 bankruptcy.
maggie-bluffs.descriptor: Casual waterfront grill at Elliott Bay Marina in Magnolia

mamma-melina.text: Three brothers who emigrated from Italy opened Mamma Melina in the University District in 1990, and the family still runs it. The kitchen does house-made pastas and wood-fired Neapolitan pizza backed by a cellar of more than 200 wine labels, and the patio looks out over the Burke-Gilman Trail.
mamma-melina.descriptor: Family-run Italian ristorante and pizzeria in the U District since 1990

maneki.text: Maneki opened in Seattle's Japantown in 1904 and is recognized as one of the oldest sushi restaurants in the United States. The original castle-shaped building seated up to 500 and had kimono-clad staff, but it was looted and vandalized during World War II, while the Sato family, who bought the restaurant in 1923, were incarcerated; they reopened in the old storage building it still occupies. It took a James Beard award in 2008.
maneki.descriptor: Japanese restaurant and sushi bar in Japantown, open since 1904

maono-fried-chicken.text: Chef Mark Fuller built Ma'ono around his grandmother's "picnic chicken" from the Kauai summers of his childhood — buttermilk-fried with Hawaiian-inspired seasoning. The signature sandwich adds bread-and-butter takuan on a butter-toasted King's Hawaiian bun. The University Village counter shares its space with Rachel's Ginger Beer.
maono-fried-chicken.descriptor: Hawaiian-style fried chicken counter at University Village

marination.text: Marination began in 2009 as a single food truck — "Big Blue" — launched by owners Kamala and Roz, and grew into a small chain of Hawaiian-Korean spots around Seattle. The 6th & Virginia shop at 2000 6th Avenue is its downtown outpost, with indoor and sidewalk seating and a weekday happy hour.
marination.descriptor: Hawaiian-Korean street food at 6th & Virginia, from a 2009 food truck

marination-ma-kai.text: Marination ma kai shares its address, 1660 Harbor Ave SW, with the West Seattle Water Taxi terminal at Seacrest Park — so the waterfront patio looks back at the downtown skyline that's a 10-to-15-minute boat ride away. It's the Alki-side, weekend-brunch branch of the Hawaiian-Korean chain that started as a 2009 food truck.
marination-ma-kai.descriptor: Hawaiian-Korean waterfront patio at Seacrest Park's water taxi dock

maripili.text: MariPili is chef Grayson Corrales's debut restaurant, a tapas bar built around the food of Galicia in northwest Spain — patatas bravas, pulpo, lamb and pork albóndigas, roasted Cornish game hen and paella tahdig — with Estrella Galicia to drink alongside it.
maripili.descriptor: Galician-inspired Spanish tapas bar on 12th Ave, Capitol Hill

market-theater.text: The Market Theater has been home to Unexpected Productions' Theatresports improv since the troupe moved in during May 1991. The bricks outside are Seattle's Gum Wall: it started in the 1990s when people queuing for shows stuck gum — with pennies pressed in — to the wall. The market stopped fighting it around 1999, and a 2015 steam cleaning scraped off more than 2,350 pounds.
market-theater.descriptor: Improv theater at 1428 Post Alley; the Gum Wall is on its alley wall

martin-luther-king-junior-civil-rights-m.text: The centerpiece of this 4.5-acre hillside park is Robert Kelly's 30-foot sculpture, inspired by King's "I've Been to the Mountaintop" speech and given to the city by the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Committee at a dedication in November 1991. The slopes around it look out over Rainier Valley, and "Civil Rights" was added to the park's official name in 2018.
martin-luther-king-junior-civil-rights-m.descriptor: 4.5-acre hillside park off MLK Jr Way S with a 30-foot King memorial

writtenFor.name: Martin Luther King Junior Civil Rights Memorial Park

mashiko.text: Opened in 1994, Mashiko threw out its conventional menu in 2009 and committed to serving only sustainable seafood — one of the first US sushi bars to convert. Two longtime employees bought the place in 2019 and kept the seafood rules intact.
mashiko.descriptor: Sustainable sushi bar on California Ave SW in West Seattle, since 1994

matador.text: The Matador has held this storefront at 5410 Ballard Ave NW since 2004, on the brick strip of Ballard Avenue. It leans as much on tequila as on its Mexican menu, and runs a second late happy hour daily from 10pm to close on top of the 4–6pm one.
matador.descriptor: Mexican food and tequila bar on Ballard Ave NW since 2004

matador-ballard.text: Nate Opper and Zak Melang started The Matador in Seattle in 2004. Melang makes the ironwork and cuts the bar and table tops for each restaurant himself, and commissions local artists to paint the mounted bull skulls that serve as the chain's emblem, so no two Matadors look alike. The draw is the tequila and agave-spirit list.
matador-ballard.descriptor: Scratch-made Mexican food and a deep tequila list, West Seattle

matts-in-the-market.text: Matt's is a small dining room on the top floor of the Corner Market Building, looking out over Pike Place. The menu changes daily around whatever the Market's vendors have that morning — the restaurant's take on the Market's 'meet the producer' tradition — and owner Dan Bugge came to it after working at Pike Place Fish.
matts-in-the-market.descriptor: Northwest seasonal dining upstairs in Pike Place's Corner Market Building

maximilien.text: A French dining room tucked into Pike Place Market since 1977, with big bay windows over Elliott Bay, West Seattle and the Olympics. It has been owner-operated since 1997, still turning out classic technique — duck confit and the like — on a seasonal, locally sourced menu.
maximilien.descriptor: French restaurant in Pike Place Market with an Elliott Bay view, since 1977

mccaw-hall.text: The hall began as the 1928 Civic Auditorium, was rebuilt as the Seattle Opera House for the 1962 World's Fair, and reopened in 2003 after a $90 million renovation. It was renamed for Marion Oliver McCaw after her four sons, including Craig McCaw, gave $20 million in her honor. Seattle Opera and Pacific Northwest Ballet both perform on its 2,963-seat stage.
mccaw-hall.descriptor: Seattle Center opera house, home to Seattle Opera and Pacific Northwest Ballet

mecca-cafe-bar.text: One of Seattle's oldest continuously operating bars, opened in 1930 by C. Preston and Frances Smith and run by the family until 2001. Half the long, skinny room is a ketchup-on-the-table diner; the other half is the bar, where decades of scribbled-on beer mats line the walls.
mecca-cafe-bar.descriptor: Diner and dive bar on Queen Anne Ave N, open since 1930

mee-sum-pastry.text: Jack and Melissa Fong run this Pike Place counter mostly on family recipes, and the draw is hum bao — big steamed buns, with the barbecue pork version the one people queue for. It's been in the Market about four decades and also has a café in the University District.
mee-sum-pastry.descriptor: Chinese bakery counter on Pike Place known for BBQ pork hum bao

mee-sum-pastry-downtown.text: Mee Sum Pastry has two Seattle locations: a University District cafe and the tiny Pike Place Market storefront famed for its giant hum bao — "eminently portable meat- or vegetable-filled steamed buns." Pineapple buns, hom bow, shumai and oversized potstickers round out the grab-and-go counter, which Eater Seattle listed among the region's notable dim sum spots in 2021.
mee-sum-pastry-downtown.descriptor: Chinese bun and pastry counter in the University District, known for hum bao

merchants-cafe-and-saloon.text: The Merchants Café is widely called Seattle's oldest restaurant, a Pioneer Square survivor. The upper floors were once a brothel, and the current owners lean hard into the building's hauntings: legend says a manager named Otto who worked there in the early 1900s still switches off the TVs and knocks bottles off the rack above the safe until he's left a glass of whiskey.
merchants-cafe-and-saloon.descriptor: Pioneer Square saloon billed as Seattle's oldest restaurant

metropolitan-grill.text: Downtown's classic steakhouse has held the corner of Second and Marion in the historic Marion Building since 1983, serving custom dry-aged USDA Prime alongside Japanese A5 wagyu. Its wine list has won Wine Spectator's Grand Award nine years running — a distinction only 99 restaurants worldwide hold.
metropolitan-grill.descriptor: Classic downtown steakhouse at 2nd & Marion since 1983

mighty-o-donuts.text: Mighty-O has made organic donuts with no chemicals, no GMOs and no animal products since 2000, starting in a Seattle basement and selling at street fairs and the Fremont Sunday Market before opening its bakery in Wallingford's historic Keystone building in 2003. This is the downtown counter at 2nd & Madison.
mighty-o-donuts.descriptor: Organic vegan donut counter at 2nd & Madison downtown

mighty-o-donuts-ballard.text: Ryan Kellner started Mighty-O in 2000 selling organic, entirely plant-based doughnuts at Seattle's University District Street Fair, opening the first storefront in 2003; the Ballard cafe followed in 2015. Bon Appétit named it one of the ten best doughnut shops in the country, and PETA called it the best vegan-friendly doughnut shop in the US.
mighty-o-donuts-ballard.descriptor: All-vegan organic doughnut shop in Ballard

mighty-o-donuts-downtown.text: Mighty-O started in May 2000 as a stand at a University District street fair and other Seattle markets, and opened its first bricks-and-mortar shop in Wallingford in 2003. Everything is plant-based, organic and non-GMO — no artificial colors, dyes or preservatives — and it has the hardware to match: Bon Appétit named it one of the ten best donut shops in the US in 2010, the same year it won Food Network Challenge's Donut Champions.
mighty-o-donuts-downtown.descriptor: All-vegan organic donut shop on N 55th St, listed as Mighty-O's Green Lake cafe

mikes-chili-parlor.text: Mike's opened in 1922, started by a Greek immigrant who sold chili from a cart in Ballard before going permanent; the family put up the brick building in 1939. His great-grandson, a fourth-generation Mike Semandiris, runs it now on the same recipe passed down by demonstration and never written down, and the City of Seattle issued a proclamation for its 100th year in 2022.
mikes-chili-parlor.descriptor: Century-old Ballard chili parlor and burger joint, family-run since 1922

mikes-noodle-house.text: This Maynard Avenue counter is known for wonton noodle soup, congee with beef or thousand-year egg, and youtiao. Eater Seattle's Jay Friedman has featured it on lists of the city's essential Asian noodle and dumpling destinations, and it draws especially large crowds on weekends; Seattle magazine once called its wonton soup with chili sauce and vinegar "perfection."
mikes-noodle-house.descriptor: Chinese wonton, congee and noodle shop on Maynard Ave in the C-ID

milstead-co.text: Andrew Milstead, a competition-level barista, opened this Fremont café in September 2011 as a multi-roaster — no house roast, just rotating beans from names like Stumptown, Intelligentsia and Coava, the Portland microroaster Milstead was the first in Seattle to pour regularly.
milstead-co.descriptor: Multi-roaster coffee bar on N 34th St in Fremont since 2011

mioposto.text: Mioposto started in 2006 as a family-owned "date-night pizzeria" in Mount Baker and has grown to five neighborhood spots around Seattle and Mercer Island. The Ravenna room keeps the same formula — open-flame cooking, signature wood-fired pizzas, and no reservations.
mioposto.descriptor: Wood-fired neighborhood pizzeria at NE 55th and 35th Ave NE in Ravenna

mioposto-north-admiral.text: Mioposto started in Mount Baker in 2006 and has stayed a family-owned, one-neighborhood-at-a-time operation, now five pizzerias around Seattle. The Eastlake room is built around a pizza bar with front-row views of the open kitchen and its signature open-flame oven, plus a copper-top bar and a heated patio that takes dogs.
mioposto-north-admiral.descriptor: Open-flame pizzeria on Eastlake Ave E with a heated dog-friendly patio

mioposto-pizzeria.text: Mioposto started in Mount Baker in 2006, and the North Admiral shop was the family-owned mini-chain's third neighborhood location. The draw is open-flame pizza plus antipasti, pasta and house-made limoncello.
mioposto-pizzeria.descriptor: Wood-fired pizza and Italian small plates on California Ave SW, North Admiral

momiji.text: Momiji opened on Capitol Hill in 2011 and hides a garden courtyard behind the dining room — a quiet counterpoint to the 12th Avenue bar strip outside. The rest of the room runs to red walls, tin ceilings, cherrywood tables and a front bar seating about 24; the kitchen is known for sushi and sashimi, grilled squid, oyster shooters and yakisoba. A South Lake Union sibling followed in 2021.
momiji.descriptor: Japanese sushi with a garden courtyard on 12th Ave, Capitol Hill, since 2011

monorail-espresso.text: Chuck Beek rolled this cart out at Westlake on December 1, 1980, and it is credited as the first espresso cart in the world. It moved repeatedly as downtown construction and location troubles pushed it around, became a permanent walk-up window in 1997, and now has four downtown locations.
monorail-espresso.descriptor: Walk-up espresso window on Pike Street, the original 1980 espresso cart

monsoon.text: Siblings Eric and Sophie Banh opened Monsoon on Capitol Hill in 1999, serving traditional Vietnamese cooking blended with Pacific Northwest ingredients. Sophie Banh, owner and head chef, is known for her pho, and the menu runs to catfish clay pot with fresh coconut juice, lemongrass gulf prawns and coconut creme caramel. The restaurant is part of the Saigon Siblings group, which also runs Ba Bar.
monsoon.descriptor: Vietnamese restaurant on 19th Ave E in Capitol Hill, open since 1999

montlake-bridge.text: Opened in June 1925, the Montlake Bridge carries Montlake Boulevard (SR 513) over Seattle's Montlake Cut, and its Collegiate Gothic control towers were styled to match Carl F. Gould's University of Washington campus just across the water. Its unusual trunnion supports were used to avoid a patent-infringement suit from the Strauss Bascule Bridge Company. It's a Seattle Landmark and joined the National Register in 1982.
montlake-bridge.descriptor: 1925 bascule drawbridge over the Montlake Cut

montlake-cut.text: Indigenous people portaged canoes across this neck of land for centuries before engineers finished the job: the Cut opened in 1916 as part of the Lake Washington Ship Canal, lowering Lake Washington 8.8 feet and drying up the Black River. Today it is University of Washington rowing water, and the gauntlet the Opening Day boat parade runs on the first Saturday in May.
montlake-cut.descriptor: Half-mile ship-canal channel between Portage and Union bays by the UW

moore-coffee.text: Moore Coffee sits right next to the Moore Theatre on Second Avenue and built its reputation on kawaii latte art. A 2021 redesign gave the room an upscale Mexico City look and added handmade tamales and churro waffles to the sandwich-and-breakfast menu.
moore-coffee.descriptor: Belltown coffee shop next door to the Moore Theatre, known for cute latte art

moore-theater.text: Real estate developer James A. Moore built the Moore in 1907 as a showplace for Gilded Age Seattle, and it's still the city's oldest active theater. Its stage runs through grunge history: Soundgarden recorded an EP there in 1988, Alice in Chains filmed a home video in 1990, and Pearl Jam shot a music video at a 1992 show.
moore-theater.descriptor: 1907 theater at 2nd and Virginia, Seattle's oldest still-active stage

mopop-museum-of-pop-culture.text: Paul Allen opened it in 2000 as the Experience Music Project, built around the world's largest collection of Jimi Hendrix artifacts, lyrics, instruments and photographs; it was renamed the Museum of Pop Culture in November 2016. Frank Gehry shaped the crumpled metal shell from electric guitars — "we started collecting pictures of Stratocasters, bringing in guitar bodies" — and the Seattle Center Monorail runs straight through the building.
mopop-museum-of-pop-culture.descriptor: Frank Gehry-designed pop culture museum at Seattle Center

moto-junction.text: Lee Kindell and Nancy Gambin were running a Belltown hostel when the pandemic shut it down, so they pivoted to pizza out of a 500-square-foot West Seattle space. Moto describes its pies as "a delightfully odd mix of Detroit, New York, Roman, and Filipino goodness," and has since grown to nine locations, including a seasonal stand inside T-Mobile Park.
moto-junction.descriptor: Detroit-meets-Filipino pan pizza in West Seattle

mox-boarding-house.text: Mox is more than 7,000 square feet of game shop — board games, Magic: The Gathering, RPGs, miniatures — wrapped around Cafe Mox, its own bar and kitchen. You can pull almost anything off the shelves and play it at your table for free while you eat.
mox-boarding-house.descriptor: Ballard board-game store with an attached café and bar on Leary Ave NW

mr-ds-greek-delicacies.text: Owner Demetrios Moraitis has run this walk-up Greek counter in Pike Place Market for more than four decades, and he is nearly as known for a sideline: sculpting busts out of raw gyro meat. His lamb portraits have included Market savior Victor Steinbrueck, Zorba the Greek, Barack Obama, and a Clinton-Trump matchup for the 2016 election.
mr-ds-greek-delicacies.descriptor: Greek gyro window in Pike Place Market's Triangle Building

murphys.descriptor: Irish pub on N 45th St in Wallingford

musang.text: Chef Melissa Miranda started Musang as a brunch pop-up series in 2017 and opened the Beacon Hill restaurant in early 2020 — right before COVID shut it down. Instead of closing, the kitchen became a community kitchen handing out more than 200 free meals a day. It was Seattle Met's Restaurant of the Year in 2020, and Food & Wine named Miranda one of its best new chefs.
musang.descriptor: Filipino restaurant on Beacon Hill from chef Melissa Miranda

musashis.descriptor: Small neighborhood sushi bar on N 45th St in Wallingford

museum-of-history-and-industry.text: Founded in 1952, MOHAI holds nearly four million artifacts of Seattle and Puget Sound history — among them Boeing's first commercial plane, the 1919 B-1, and the 12-foot neon "R" from the Rainier Brewery. Only about 2% is on display at a time. The museum left its Montlake home ahead of the SR 520 rebuild and reopened here in December 2012 after a $90 million restoration of the armory.
museum-of-history-and-industry.descriptor: Seattle history museum in the old Naval Reserve Armory at Lake Union Park

mv-skansonia.text: Built in 1929 by the Skansie Brothers of Gig Harbor, the Skansonia carried cars and passengers across Puget Sound for decades and made her last crossing from Tahlequah to Point Defiance on July 20, 1967. Declared surplus and sold in 1971, she served as a private residence on Lake Washington, then was renovated as a banquet hall in the mid-1980s and moved to Lake Union, where she is billed as Seattle's last wooden ferry.
mv-skansonia.descriptor: 1929 wooden auto ferry moored on Lake Union, now a wedding venue

myrtle-edwards-park.text: Originally Elliott Bay Park, it was renamed in 1976 for the late city councilwoman Myrtle Edwards after her family asked that her name be removed from what is now Gas Works Park, disagreeing with that park's design focus. The park hosted Seattle's Fourth of Jul-Ivar's fireworks show from 1964 to 2008 and has hosted the annual Seattle Hempfest.
myrtle-edwards-park.descriptor: 4.8-acre Elliott Bay waterfront park with a 1.25-mile shoreline trail

national-nordic-museum.text: Founded in 1980 as the Nordic Heritage Museum in a former Ballard elementary school, it exhibits the art, objects and culture of Danish, Finnish, Icelandic, Norwegian and Swedish Americans and the wider Nordic region. Its 57,000-square-foot Mithun-designed building opened in May 2018 — dedicated by Iceland's president and Denmark's crown princess — and Congress designated it the National Nordic Museum in 2019.
national-nordic-museum.descriptor: Nordic art and immigration museum on NW Market Street in Ballard

navy-strength.text: Anu Apte and Chris Elford — the couple behind Rob Roy — opened Navy Strength in Belltown in 2017 to do tiki without the kitsch: an ever-changing tropical drink menu in a nautical mid-century room, with oysters and nachos to go with it.
navy-strength.descriptor: Belltown tropical and tiki cocktail bar on 2nd Ave, opened 2017

needle-thread.text: Tucked above Tavern Law in the 1919 Trace Lofts building on Capitol Hill, Needle & Thread has no menu: you tell the bartender what you like and they build a bespoke drink, one round at a time. It is reservations-first for parties up to six, 21 and over, open nightly until midnight.
needle-thread.descriptor: Reservation-only speakeasy upstairs from Tavern Law on 12th Ave

neighbours.text: Opened in 1983 at 1509 Broadway, Neighbours is Seattle's oldest still-operating LGBTQ+ club, where drag legend Crystal Lane grew the local drag and fundraising scene before her death in 1994.
neighbours.descriptor: Capitol Hill gay dance club on Broadway since 1983

neptune-theatre.text: The Neptune opened as a silent-movie house in 1921 and still wears its sea-god theme, with statues of Neptune and a concession stand shaped like a boat. It screened The Rocky Horror Picture Show weekly for 14 years starting in 1991, among the longest continuous runs in the country, before Seattle Theatre Group spent $700,000 turning it into a live venue in 2011.
neptune-theatre.descriptor: 1921 U District movie palace turned live-music venue, with Neptune statues

nippon-kan-theater.text: Built by the Nippon Kan Company and dedicated in January 1910, this hall was the hub of Seattle's Japantown — plays and touring performers from Japan, judo and kendo matches, movies and community meetings — until it was boarded up in 1942 during wartime incarceration. It was restored and reopened in 1981 and is on the National Register of Historic Places.
nippon-kan-theater.descriptor: 1909 Japantown meeting hall and theater on S Washington St

nishino.text: Chef Tatsu Nishino, a Kyoto native, trained in Osaka and cooked at Matsuhisa in Los Angeles before opening his own restaurant on East Madison Street in 1995, a short walk from the Washington Park Arboretum.
nishino.descriptor: Madison Park Japanese restaurant and sushi bar, open since 1995

noi-thai-cuisine.text: Noi Thai continues the Bai Tong restaurants, which began as a favorite stopover for Thai Airways crews at Sea-Tac Airport more than two decades ago. Owner JJ created Noi in 2002 as an homage to his wife and recruited chefs from Thailand; the plated signatures include yellow curry crab, tom yum lobster and red curry roast duck.
noi-thai-cuisine.descriptor: Upscale Thai dining room in downtown Seattle

noi-thai-cuisine-green-lake.text: Noi Thai is named for the founder's wife: "Noi" means little or tiny in Thai, a childhood nickname as the youngest daughter, and he opened the first restaurant in 2002 as a tribute to her, recruiting chefs from Thailand to cook it. The family runs deep in Northwest Thai food — Noi's mother, Chanpen Lapangkura, founded the Bai Tong restaurants back in 1989.
noi-thai-cuisine-green-lake.descriptor: Upscale Thai restaurant on East Green Lake Drive N

northwest-african-american-museum.text: The museum exists because activists occupied the abandoned Colman School in 1985 and stayed for eight years to keep the wrecking ball away. It finally opened in 2008 inside the 1909 schoolhouse, with galleries on the ground floor and 36 affordable apartments above; the inaugural show featured Jacob Lawrence and James W. Washington, Jr.
northwest-african-american-museum.descriptor: Museum in the 1909 Colman School building, Central District

northwest-film-forum.text: It started in 1995 as WigglyWorld Studios, a filmmakers' collective founded on a King County Arts Commission grant, and is now a nonprofit two-screen arthouse on 12th Ave in Capitol Hill, with workshops and youth programs alongside the screenings. Its signature event, the Local Sightings Film Festival, programs nothing but Pacific Northwest filmmakers.
northwest-film-forum.descriptor: Nonprofit two-screen arthouse cinema on 12th Ave, Capitol Hill

nue.text: Nue serves hard-to-find street food from around the world — Latvian smoked sprats, Trinidadian goat curry, Romanian mititei, a Japanese katsu sandwich on white bread with Kewpie mayo — under co-owner Uyên Nguyễn. Atlas Obscura called it one of the most adventurous dining experiences in the Pacific Northwest.
nue.descriptor: Global street-food restaurant on 14th Ave, Capitol Hill

oasis-tea-zone.text: Opened by the Liu family in 2001, Oasis bills itself as the longest-running boba shop in the Pacific Northwest. Beyond milk teas, smoothies and snacks, the CID original works as a hangout, with arcade games, board games and a pinball machine.
oasis-tea-zone.descriptor: Boba tea shop in the Chinatown-International District since 2001

occidental-square.text: Created in 1971 on the former site of the Carrollton Hotel, the Pioneer Square park hosted Seattle's first Pride Week in 1974, when around 200 LGBTQ people gathered for a picnic and dance party; the city made it the Pride parade endpoint in 1977 until the parade moved to Capitol Hill in the 1980s. Hai Ying Wu's Fallen Firefighters Memorial honors four firefighters killed in a 1995 International District warehouse fire.
occidental-square.descriptor: Pioneer Square park with the Fallen Firefighters Memorial

ocho.text: Ocho is a corner tapas bar so small and informal it's easy to walk past — no reservations, 21-and-over, first come first served. The pours lean hard Iberian (sherry, Spanish cider, Peninsula wines) next to garlicky gambas, octopus and pan con chocolate.
ocho.descriptor: Tiny Spanish tapas bar on a corner of NW Market St in Ballard

oddfellows-cafe.text: Oddfellows opened in 2008 when Linda Derschang took the ground floor of the Oddfellows Hall, a 1908 Renaissance Revival building by architect C. A. Breitung that served for decades as a cultural nucleus for Capitol Hill's community and arts organizations and still houses the Century Ballroom. Huge communal-style tables set the tone inside.
oddfellows-cafe.descriptor: All-day cafe and bar in the 1908 Oddfellows Hall at 10th & Pine

off-the-rez-cafe.text: Mark McConnell of the Blackfeet Nation and his partner Cecilia Rikard started Off the Rez in 2011 as what the Snoqualmie Valley Record calls Seattle's first Native food truck, then opened this roughly 30-seat cafe inside the Burke Museum on the UW campus in 2019. Bison frybread tacos and wild rice bowls anchor a menu that sources produce, fish and bison from tribal vendors where possible.
off-the-rez-cafe.descriptor: Native American cafe in the Burke Museum, known for bison frybread tacos

old-stove-brewing.text: Chris Moore and Brian Stan started Old Stove in 2016 and became one of the first anchor tenants of the Pike Place MarketFront, the Market's first expansion in 40 years, in 2017. Beer is brewed on site in keeping with the Market's "meet the producer" tradition, behind a window wall onto Elliott Bay and the Olympics. Seattle magazine named it best brewery taproom in 2018.
old-stove-brewing.descriptor: Brewpub at Pike Place MarketFront with a window wall onto Elliott Bay

old-stove-brewing-co-marketfront.text: Old Stove began in 2016 as an anchor brewery of Pike Place Market's MarketFront; the Gardens is its Ballard offshoot, an outdoor beer garden with fire pits and string lights, a scratch kitchen sourcing from local farms and foragers, and weekly trivia. Dogs and kids are welcome.
old-stove-brewing-co-marketfront.descriptor: Old Stove's Ballard beer garden brewpub with fire pits and string lights

olivers-lounge.text: Oliver's opened inside the Mayflower Park Hotel in 1976 as Washington's first "daylight" bar, with street-facing floor-to-ceiling windows. Fifty years on it remains one of Seattle's longest independently owned bars, and the classic martini is still what people come for.
olivers-lounge.descriptor: Martini bar in the Mayflower Park Hotel on Olive Way, downtown, since 1976

olympic-sculpture-park.text: The site belonged to the oil and gas company Unocal until the 1970s and sat as a contaminated brownfield before the Seattle Art Museum cleaned it up and opened the free nine-acre park in January 2007. Works by Alexander Calder, Richard Serra, Louise Bourgeois and Mark di Suvero step down the bluff to a rebuilt beach on Puget Sound.
olympic-sculpture-park.descriptor: Free 9-acre waterfront sculpture park run by the Seattle Art Museum

ooink-ramen.text: Ooink is the ramen shop of chef Chong Boon Ooi and his wife Jiaxin Wang, whose pig logo nods to the sliced pork The Infatuation called the most tender in town, served alongside massive gyoza. The original is a tiny room above the Broadway QFC on Capitol Hill; this second location opened in Fremont in 2022. Seattle Metropolitan put it on its 2022 list of the city's 100 best restaurants.
ooink-ramen.descriptor: Ramen shop known for tender sliced pork and oversized gyoza

osteria-la-spiga.text: Chef Sabrina Tinsley and her husband Pietro Borghesi opened la Spiga in 1998 to cook the food of Italy's Emilia-Romagna region. After eight years in a smaller space it moved into Capitol Hill's Piston & Ring building, a converted auto body shop with wooden beams and a long wine-backed bar. The house-made breads are the giveaway: la vera piadina romagnola, gnocco fritto, pane all'olio.
osteria-la-spiga.descriptor: Emilia-Romagna osteria on 12th Ave in a converted auto shop, since 1998

owl-n-thistle.text: Jack Geary and Declan Fury opened the Owl 'N Thistle in 1993 in the Coleman Building, rebuilt after Seattle's Great Fire of 1889; the pub says the foundation is a retired clipper ship, the Windward. A former Scottish proprietress, Bonnie McGregor, gave the place its name. There's live music most nights — trad Irish through jazz and funk — plus pool, darts, Guinness beef stew and fish and chips.
owl-n-thistle.descriptor: Irish pub in the historic Coleman Building with live music most nights

pacific-inn-pub.text: A Stone Way pub that has been frying fish and chips since 1981 and bills itself as "Seattle's Famous Fish & Chips." It's 21-and-over and pours until 2am, which makes it as much a late-night stop as a dinner one.
pacific-inn-pub.descriptor: Fish-and-chips pub on Stone Way in Wallingford, since 1981

pacific-science-center.text: Those arches went up as the United States Science Pavilion for the 1962 World's Fair, designed by Minoru Yamasaki — the architect who later designed New York's World Trade Center. The building stayed on as a science museum and now draws more than a million visitors a year to its IMAX theaters, laser dome, planetarium and butterfly house.
pacific-science-center.descriptor: Hands-on science museum under Yamasaki's arches at Seattle Center

pagliacci-pizza.text: Pagliacci started in 1979 as a single shop in the University District and now runs about two dozen locations in King and Snohomish counties, with Matt Galvin and Pat McDonald as owners. Its boxes have been made from FSC-certified and post-consumer recycled fiber since 2011, and it opened Seattle's first stand-alone LEED-certified pizzeria in Madison Park in 2012.
pagliacci-pizza.descriptor: Seattle pizza chain's West Seattle Junction shop on California Ave SW

paju.text: Named after the South Korean city of Paju, this modern Korean kitchen opened in 2019 and quickly became one of Seattle's most-praised restaurants — the New York Times included it on a 2021 list of the country's most exciting places to eat. Squid-ink fried rice and truffled ribeye bulgogi are the dishes people name.
paju.descriptor: Modern Korean small plates on Westlake Ave N in South Lake Union

palace-kitchen.text: Tom Douglas's third restaurant, open since 1996 and billing itself as a "tavern with good food" — U-shaped bar, dim light, burgers and goat cheese lavender fondue. Eater Seattle called it a centerpiece of Belltown and the late-night industry hangout where cooks and bartenders landed after their shifts. It went dark in March 2020 and stayed closed three years before reopening in April 2023.
palace-kitchen.descriptor: Tom Douglas tavern in Belltown with a U-shaped bar, since 1996

palermo-ballard.descriptor: Pizza restaurant at 2005 NW Market St in Ballard

pams-caribbean-kitchen.text: Pam Jacob cooks the Trinidadian food she grew up with — curry goat, oxtail, jerk chicken and wrapped roti — from a restaurant that began as a small snack shack in Trinidad. Open in Seattle since 2006, it runs karaoke on Thursdays and a live steel drum band on Fridays.
pams-caribbean-kitchen.descriptor: Trinidadian and Caribbean kitchen on N 45th St in Wallingford since 2006

panama-hotel.text: Built in 1910 by Sabro Ozasa, Seattle's first Japanese American architect, the Panama was a hub of Japantown — rooms, shops, restaurants and the Hashidate-Yu bathhouse, one of four sento in early-1900s Seattle and the last one left in the United States. Families stored their belongings in the basement before wartime incarceration and many never came back for them; a glass panel in the floor lets you look down at what's left. National Historic Landmark, 2006.
panama-hotel.descriptor: 1910 Japantown hotel and tea house with an intact basement sento

panama-hotel-tea-coffee.text: Built in 1910 by Sabro Ozasa, Seattle's first Japanese American architect, the Panama Hotel holds the Hashidate-Yu, the last intact Japanese sento bathhouse in the country. Families sent to WWII incarceration camps stored belongings in the basement; roughly 50 trunks were never claimed, and a glass panel in the tea house floor looks down on them. A National Historic Landmark since 2006, it inspired the novel Hotel on the Corner of Bitter and Sweet.
panama-hotel-tea-coffee.descriptor: Tea house in the 1910 Panama Hotel, Japantown in the Chinatown-ID

paramount-theatre.text: It opened in 1928 as the Seattle Theatre and was renamed the Paramount in 1930. The Rapp & Rapp palace still has one of only three original Publix 1 Wurlitzer organs, kept playable by volunteers from the Puget Sound Theatre Organ Society. It joined the National Register in 1974 and became a city landmark in 1995; Nirvana's 1991 concert here was shot on 16mm film.
paramount-theatre.descriptor: 1928 movie palace at 9th and Pine, now a Broadway and concert house

paseo.text: Cuban-born chef Lorenzo Lorenzo opened Paseo in Fremont in 1994, and the garlicky Cuban Roast sandwich drew weekend lines down the block; a 2010 TLC series ranked it the second-best sandwich in America. Both Paseo locations closed abruptly in November 2014 amid bankruptcy, a buyer paid $91,000 for the name at a federal auction, and staff reverse-engineered the recipes to reopen Fremont in January 2015.
paseo.descriptor: Caribbean sandwich counter in Fremont known for the Cuban Roast

paseo-sodo.text: Paseo began in 1994 as a tiny cash-only Fremont window whose Caribbean pork sandwiches drew weekend lines. Both shops closed abruptly in November 2014; a buyer took the name and assets at auction for $91,000 and reverse-engineered the recipes without the founder's help, reopening in January 2015. This SODO shop followed in July 2016.
paseo-sodo.descriptor: Caribbean sandwich counter on 1st Ave S, known for garlicky roast pork

pecado-bueno-fremont.descriptor: From-scratch Mexican restaurant at 4307 Fremont Ave N

pelmeni-dumpling-tzar.text: The menu is essentially one thing: pel'meni, beef or potato, buried in sour cream and spices with a slice of rye bread on the side. It sits steps from Fremont's Lenin statue and stays open past 2 a.m., which has made it the neighborhood's default post-drinking stop.
pelmeni-dumpling-tzar.descriptor: Late-night Russian dumpling counter on Fremont Place, by the Lenin statue

pestle-rock.text: Pestle Rock cooks Isan food from Thailand's northeast on Ballard's NW Market Street, and the name is literal — "rocking" the pestle is how the spice pastes that define the region get made. The house line is to eat the way Isan people do: with your hands, mixing and dipping in a range of authentic sauces, because "more messy means more delicious."
pestle-rock.descriptor: Isan (Northeast Thai) kitchen on NW Market Street in Ballard

petes-eggnest.text: Pete's Eggnest is the Seattle arm of a family-owned breakfast group whose siblings, The Egg & Us and 12th Avenue Cafe, are both in Issaquah. It sticks to "cozy and comforting breakfast staples" and closes at 2pm on weekdays, 3pm on weekends.
petes-eggnest.descriptor: Family-run breakfast and brunch spot on Greenwood Ave N

phnom-penh-noodle-house.text: Sam Ung opened Phnom Penh in 1987 in the Chinatown-International District, starting with seven noodle dishes; it was described in 2020 as Seattle's only Cambodian restaurant. The family closed it in 2018 and reopened after two years in August 2020. Kuyteav and beef lok lak are the dishes it is known for.
phnom-penh-noodle-house.descriptor: Cambodian noodle house on S Jackson St in the C-ID, since 1987

pho-bac.text: Phở Bắc started in 1982 as Cat's Submarine Sandwich Shop until the Vietnamese community talked the owners into serving phở instead. The Pham family has run it ever since and were James Beard semifinalists for Outstanding Restaurateur in 2023; a downtown location opened in 2021 with an upstairs bar called Phởcific Standard Time. The original in the ID is the red boat-shaped building.
pho-bac.descriptor: Downtown outpost of Seattle's Phở Bắc, Vietnamese pho since 1982

pho-bac-sup-shop.text: The Pham family's Phở Bắc started in 1982 as Cat's Submarine Sandwich Shop in the Chinatown–International District; four months after phở went on the menu it had taken over, and the name changed with it. Súp Shop opened on New Year's Day 2018, near the family's original red boat-shaped building on S Jackson St. The Phams were James Beard Outstanding Restaurateur semifinalists in 2023.
pho-bac-sup-shop.descriptor: Phở shop in Little Saigon, from the family behind Seattle's Phở Bắc

pho-than-brothers.descriptor: Pho-only Vietnamese noodle shop near Green Lake, cream puffs for dessert

pie-bar.text: Pie Bar has been pairing slices with a drink chaser on E Olive Way since 2013 and calls itself the world's original pie bar. The crossover is the whole point — banana cream, mud pie and coconut cream next to a lineup of 'pietini' cocktails — and it runs late, until 2 a.m. on weekends.
pie-bar.descriptor: Late-night pie-and-cocktail bar on E Olive Way, Capitol Hill

pier-62.text: Built in 1901 as the Gaffney Dock, Pier 62 was acquired by the city in 1989 and spent years as the stage for the Summer Nights at the Pier concert series, until the aging timber piles could no longer carry a stage and a crowd. Rebuilt on roughly 175 steel legs starting in 2017, it reopened in September 2020 as the first piece of the new Waterfront Park, and now hosts free performances, yoga and firepit socials.
pier-62.descriptor: Rebuilt 1901 pier, now a public deck and event space on Waterfront Park

pike-place-chowder.text: Larry Mellum and Mike Hillyer opened the Post Alley window in 2003, after working up the recipe in the 1990s at a West Seattle cafe. Their New England clam chowder has won repeatedly at chowder cook-offs on both coasts, and the shop counts 17 national chowder titles.
pike-place-chowder.descriptor: Chowder counter in Post Alley at Pike Place Market since 2003

pike-place-chowder-downtown-pine-street.text: Larry Mellum and chef Mike Hillyer spent the 1990s refining a New England clam chowder at a small West Seattle kitchen, then opened in Pike Place Market's Post Alley in 2003. Their chowder has since taken 17 national first-place titles; this Pine Street shop is the Pacific Place location.
pike-place-chowder-downtown-pine-street.descriptor: Chowder bar in Pacific Place on Pine St downtown

pike-place-market.text: Opened on August 17, 1907, it's one of the oldest continuously operated public farmers markets in the country and Seattle's most-visited attraction, drawing over 20 million people a year. The original Starbucks (1971, moved to 1912 Pike Place in 1977) is here, the Pike Place Fish Market crew still throws salmon over the counter, and a bronze piggy bank named Rachel collects thousands a year for market social services.
pike-place-market.descriptor: Public farmers market above Elliott Bay, open since 1907

pinoyshki-bakery-cafe.text: It started in 1994 as Piroshki on 3rd downtown; Aly Anderson took it over in 2016 and began crossing Russian piroshki dough with Filipino fillings like garlic beef asado, alongside sides such as atsara. Guy Fieri filmed it for Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives in 2018, and it rebranded as Pinoyshki in December 2023 before moving to East Pine on Capitol Hill in early 2024.
pinoyshki-bakery-cafe.descriptor: Filipino-Russian piroshki bakery on E Pine, Capitol Hill

pioneer-building.text: Elmer Fisher's Pioneer Building went up in 1892 at 600 First Avenue; when the plans were unveiled in 1888 the local press predicted it would be one of the finest buildings in the country and the largest north of San Francisco. During the 1897 Klondike gold rush, 48 mining companies kept offices inside. It's a National Historic Landmark and the launch point for the Underground Tour.
pioneer-building.descriptor: 1892 Richardsonian Romanesque landmark on First Ave, Pioneer Square

pioneer-square.text: This wedge of brick marks Seattle's original downtown, rebuilt in Richardsonian Romanesque stone and brick after the Great Fire of 1889 and booming as an outfitting hub for the 1897 Klondike gold rush. The 1909 cast-iron-and-glass pergola sheltered cable-car riders and sat atop an underground restroom once called the most lavish west of the Mississippi; it was made a National Historic Landmark in 1977 along with the totem pole and Pioneer Building.
pioneer-square.descriptor: Triangular park at 1st & Yesler with an iron pergola and totem pole

pioneer-square-pergola.text: Built in 1909 by architect Julian Everett, the pergola sheltered cable-car riders and capped an underground public restroom praised at the time as the most lavish west of the Mississippi. A semi-truck destroyed it on January 15, 2001; the city rebuilt it using about 99% original material and reopened it in August 2002. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1977 along with the adjacent Pioneer Building and totem pole.
pioneer-square-pergola.descriptor: 1909 cast-iron and glass cable-car shelter in Pioneer Square

piroshky-piroshky.text: Vladimir and Zina Kotelnikov opened Piroshky Piroshky at Pike Place in 1992, selling savory and sweet Russian hand pies - beef and cheese, chicken pot pie, cinnamon-cardamom braids. Anthony Bourdain filmed there for No Reservations in 2007, and Smithsonian magazine put it on a 2013 list of iconic American food destinations.
piroshky-piroshky.descriptor: Russian piroshky bakery at Pike Place Market since 1992

pizza-pi-vegan-pizzeria.text: Pizza Pi is entirely plant-based and bills itself as "America's oldest vegan pizzeria." Its Roosevelt Way NE counter turns out pies like the E.M.P. — short for "Experience More Plants" — built on pesto and potatoes.
pizza-pi-vegan-pizzeria.descriptor: All-vegan pizzeria on Roosevelt Way NE near the U District

pony.text: Pony occupies a steel former Associated gas station on E Madison — the bar's own dating puts it in the 1940s, Wikipedia in the 1930s — with a roofed, west-facing patio kept usable year-round by a gas fire pit and electric heaters. It's styled as a tribute to 1970s West Village and Castro bars, and Seattle Weekly readers voted it the city's best gay bar in 2013.
pony.descriptor: Gay dive bar in a converted 1940s gas station on E Madison

poquitos.text: Poquitos opened at 10th and Pike in 2011 under Deming Maclise and James Weimann and has been a Capitol Hill fixture since — Seattle Metropolitan named it one of the best restaurants on the Hill in 2021. The LGBTQ-owned business later expanded to Bothell in 2018 (closed September 2025) and Tacoma in 2022.
poquitos.descriptor: Mexican restaurant at 10th & Pike on Capitol Hill since 2011

port-of-seattle-fishermens-terminal.text: Opened in 1914 on Salmon Bay, it has been the home port of Seattle's commercial fishing fleet ever since, with moorage for more than 700 vessels including boats seen on Deadliest Catch. The Seattle Fishermen's Memorial there carries plaques naming more than 670 local commercial fishermen and women lost at sea since the beginning of the 20th century.
port-of-seattle-fishermens-terminal.descriptor: Port of Seattle home port of the North Pacific fishing fleet on Salmon Bay

portage-bay-cafe.text: Portage Bay Cafe has been doing Seattle breakfast and brunch since 1997, built around a local-organic-sustainable sourcing pledge it sums up as "eat like you give a damn." The South Lake Union café is one of five locations, alongside Roosevelt, Ballard, 65th and West Seattle.
portage-bay-cafe.descriptor: South Lake Union breakfast and brunch spot, organic and local since 1997

portage-bay-cafe-and-catering.text: Portage Bay Cafe started in 1997 on an "eat like you give a damn" premise — local, organic, sustainable — and now runs five Seattle-area cafes. The Roosevelt Way NE location serves the University District, and the house move is ordering house-made pancakes or French toast so you get a run at the fresh toppings bar.
portage-bay-cafe-and-catering.descriptor: Organic breakfast cafe on Roosevelt Way NE with a fresh toppings bar

portage-bay-cafe-roosevelt.text: Portage Bay Cafe started in 1997 with a "local, organic, sustainable" pledge it still prints as "eat like you give a damn." The Ballard room at 2821 NW Market St is billed as "a more cozy version of our cafes" and sits next to the Ballard Locks; the original is at 4130 Roosevelt Way NE.
portage-bay-cafe-roosevelt.descriptor: Organic breakfast and brunch cafe on NW Market St near the Ballard Locks

portage-bay-cafe-university-district.text: Portage Bay Cafe opened in 1997 around the motto "eat like you give a damn," built on local, organic and sustainable sourcing, and is known for its breakfast toppings bar. It has since grown to five Seattle-area cafes; this is the Roosevelt one, on NE 65th St.
portage-bay-cafe-university-district.descriptor: Organic breakfast and brunch cafe on NE 65th St in Roosevelt

post-alley-pizza.text: It's one of the businesses lining Post Alley, the 2,000-foot brick lane running from Virginia to Seneca that Wikipedia calls Seattle's best-known alley — named for the city's first post office, opened in 1880, and home to Pike Place Market's Gum Wall.
post-alley-pizza.descriptor: Pizzeria in Post Alley, downtown Seattle's brick-paved market lane

prost.text: Chris Navarra opened Prost! on Greenwood Avenue on September 5, 2002, billing it as Seattle's original German pub — the place that introduced the city to German beer poured properly, with a head, in traditional glassware. Bratwurst and big steins are the point.
prost.descriptor: German pub on Greenwood Ave in Phinney Ridge, open since 2002

public-market-clock.text: The clock and red neon 'Public Market Center' sign mark the main entrance to Pike Place Market, which opened August 17, 1907 so shoppers could 'meet the producer' and drew nearly 21 million visitors in 2023 — Seattle's most popular tourist destination. Near the entrance sits Rachel, a 550-pound bronze piggy bank by Georgia Gerber dedicated in 1986; the coins dropped in her fund market social services.
public-market-clock.descriptor: Neon 'Public Market Center' clock over Pike Place Market's main entrance

purple-cafe-and-wine-bar-seattle.text: Heavy Restaurant Group's downtown Purple is built around a thirty-foot wine tower in the middle of the dining room, seen through floor-to-ceiling glass, a block from the 5th Avenue Theatre and Benaroya Hall. It is marking its 20th anniversary; the Woodinville original that launched the group is five years older.
purple-cafe-and-wine-bar-seattle.descriptor: Wine bar at 1225 4th Ave with a 30-foot wine tower in the dining room

writtenFor.name: Purple Cafe and Wine Bar - Seattle

queen-anne-beerhall.descriptor: German-style beer hall near Seattle Center with 25+ taps

queen-mary-tea-room.text: "Queen" Mary Greengo opened the tea room in 1988, and it is now one of the oldest independent tea rooms in the country — it appears in Bruce Richardson's "The Great Tea Rooms of America," and CNN Travel named it one of five great American tea rooms. Greengo's stated aim: "I want people to feel warm and welcomed here, not stuffy."
queen-mary-tea-room.descriptor: English afternoon tea room on NE 55th St in Ravenna since 1988

quinns.text: Scott and Heather Staples opened Quinn's in 2007 as a Capitol Hill take on the 1990s London gastropub; brothers Charles and Peter Kim took it over in 2018. The wild boar sloppy joe is the dish people name first — Eater Seattle put it on a 2014 list of iconic Seattle meat dishes — and Anthony Bourdain filmed here for a 2013 episode of The Layover.
quinns.descriptor: Gastropub at 10th & Pike on Capitol Hill, open since 2007

rachels-ginger-beer-pike-place-market.text: Rachel Marshall was introduced to ginger beer in Germany, started brewing it in Seattle, and sold it at farmers' markets and a Pike Place stall before opening this flagship shop in the Market in July 2013 with partner Adam Peters. Artist Stacey Rozich designed the murals in all four Seattle locations.
rachels-ginger-beer-pike-place-market.descriptor: Fresh-ginger ginger beer shop in Pike Place Market, open since 2013
